subsubtopic: RESEARCH INTO PREVENTION AND CURE OF SCHIZOPHRENIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition on behalf of 253 residents of the Kitchener-Waterloo area in respect of the disorder schizophrenia. The petitioners consider schizophrenia to be a major illness in Canada, affecting about one per cent of the population, and they call upon the Parliament of Canada to put into place research efforts which are commensurate with the fact of schizophrenia being a major illness in Canada.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF RIGHTS OF THE UNBORN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to present a petition organized by the Pentecostal Church of Fort Smith, Northwest Territories. The prayer of the petition calls upon Parliament to pass into law legislation
that will protect the life of the unborn child from conception and through all stages of development, with the exception of the extremely rare situation in which an abortion is performed in order to save the life of the mother.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN OWNERSHIP OF UTILITIES, DAMS AND WATER LICENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition from several residents of the southern Okanagan Valley of British Columbia. The petition asks Parliament to pass a law requiring majority ownership by Canadians of electrical utilities, dams and water licences so that Canadian citizens will be afforded sovereignty protection equal to that enjoyed by citizens of the United States in respect of electrical utilities in that country.

That this House condemn the government for its total and absolute failure
to provide fair and equitable postal service to all Canadians by:
(a)	instructing Canada Post to cut back postal services to Canadians living in rural areas;
(b)	installing "supermailboxes" to take the place of door-to-door mail delivery in new suburban areas; and
(c)	making hundreds of thousands of Canadians second-class citizens when it comes to the provision of postal service.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the outset I move this motion in the absence of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) who could not be here today. He is the official spokesperson for my Party on matters concerning the Post Office. As you probably know, the Hon. Member has done a tremendous job over the last several years in ensuring that the words of concern of those who have been denied postal service have been brought forward in the House of Commons. These concerns have been heard.
Post Office bashing in this country has become a national pastime primarily because of the actions of the Government. The Post Office has been involved recently in slashing services and by doing so it has made an already bad situation worse. It has come to my attention as well that sometime later today,
probably at three o'clock, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) will be tabling in the House Canada Post's corporate plan, which will be followed by a press conference at 3.30 p.m., I believe, in which the Minister will attempt to convince Canadians that the policies and the actions of the Government respecting Canada Post have been the best thing since sliced bread.
As I understand it from what I hear through the rumour mill, the Minister will try to tell Canadians that for the first time in some years Canada Post will be breaking even. Yet, several months ago, the same Minister was trying to tell Canadians that Canada Post in this year alone would be making a profit of some $20 million. He will also tell us that Canada Post will continue with its supermailbox plan. He will go on to say, of course, after all that bad news-from his point of view good news-that Canadians will be faced with another increase in postal rates. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that that will do absolutely nothing to improve the image of Canada Post across Canada.
I want to talk for a brief moment about what Canada Post has been doing in my own constituency and, indeed, in constituencies right across the land. About 18 months ago trucks appeared suddenly on the main drags in my own area and started picking up the corner mailboxes. They are being picked up in Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto and St. John's, Newfoundland, in fact, right across the country. Canada Post claimed that corner mailboxes were not being used to their fullest extent possible. But there was absolutely no consultation with Members of Parliament representing the areas or with the communities involved.
It was a totally arbitrary action taken by Canada Post. An owner of a corner store in my community, when he saw the truck picking up the mail box, went out to those doing it and asked them why. The guy said, "This mail box is not being used as much as it was in recent years. Therefore, we are removing it". The corner store owner asked them to open up the mail box to let him see what was in it. The box was practically full, but there it went on the back of a truck and it was gone. I got in touch with the public relations people at Canada Post in Toronto and asked them why they were picking up boxes. They repeated the same story, that mailboxes were not being used. Even when they heard that the particular mail box to which I was referring was being used they said, "The facts of life these days are that people no longer use corner mailboxes. Most people in Toronto work downtown and they take their mail downtown with them to their places of work and mail the letters there".
I have one of the largest senior citizen populations of any constituency in the country. These people do not work downtown. In fact, they do not work. They are retired. Canada Post's removal of these corner mailboxes is causing all kinds of problems for seniors in my community, especially if they happen to have a mobility problem. It is bad enough in the summer months when seniors have to walk several blocks to mail a letter, but in the winter when the sidewalks are icy or
May 12, 1988

snow-covered it places a severe hardship upon them. It is bad enough in a place like Toronto, but when you go into some of the more remote areas of Canada where Canada Post is cutting service and where the winter is longer, communities lack sidewalks and that kind of thing, it is worse. Canada Post has made life extremely difficult for people with mobility problems, whether as a result of old age or disability.
In addition to that, there is a franchising or privatization of postal service which has resulted in the closing of a whole slew of sub-post stations in rural Canada. It is resulting in the closing of postal stations in areas like Toronto where people used to pick up parcels at corner stores that were fairly close to the places where they resided. Canada Post has closed those places up. In my own community, some people have to go about a mile out of their way now in order to pick up a parcel that they would have picked up within several blocks of their residences or sometimes a little further. That is what Canada Post has been doing.
In addition to that, as if Canada Post was not happy enough with that, it discontinued door-to-door delivery service in new subdivisions. They have supermailboxes now to which people have to go to pick up their mail rather than door-to-door delivery. In my own community, there is a new subdivision that faces onto a well established neighbourhood. The people on one block receive door-to-door delivery services and yet those a block away have to go to the supermailbox in order to pick up their mail.
The Government has made a whole number of Canadians feel like second-class citizens. They do feel as though they were second-class citizens. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), will be speaking at some length about the problems faced by Canadian citizens who happen to live in rural communities and about the difficulties Canada Post has created for those Canadians.
For those who live in rural Canada, the closure of rural post offices is not just an economic move by Canada Post. For those people, the post offices are very often the centres of the communities.
And they are killing communities.

When Canada Post arbitrarily closes down post offices, it is taking away a way of life that Canadians in this vast, diverse land have become used to. Not only have they become used to it but they have viewed the post office as the centre of life in their communities.
A resident of one of these communities has described in a very eloquent way what those post offices mean to life in those communities. This lady, who happens to live in Little Fort, British Columbia, wrote to her Member of Parliament. She said:
The post office is where we learn about births and deaths, the happy events
and sad, the everyday happenings in our village. Its postmaster is our friend

and confidante. She has her finger on the pulse of our village. Postal rates may
be high, but there is no charge for her cheerful "Good Morning". To some of
the older folk who live alone, she is their connection with reality.
That rural resident has a certain view of the role that the rural post office plays in that particular community. When Canada Post, under the instructions of this Government, arbitrarily closed that post office it was, as the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) said a second ago, literally killing that community. It was killing a whole way of life, and it is being condemned by a growing number of Canadians.
If this Government thinks that this is an issue that will go away with the passage of time, it is wrong. The people will not forget come election day. The Government is making a bad, serious mistake. This issue will not go away. It is with us. Canadians know the value of postal services in Canada, and this Government will pay dearly in the next election for its treatment of Canadians, not only in rural Canada but in urban Canada as well.
One of the reasons given by the Government for the reduction in service was given by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The only way he can see it is as an improvement in service. Only the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs could make that kind of statement and expect people to believe him.
We watched this Minister do a number of things in his capacity as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I think his job description is all wrong. He does not protect consumers. The only thing he protects is corporate interests. We saw that with the amendments to the Patent Act. He told us that that Bill was in the best interests of Canadians. I recall question after question being put to him on that particular piece of legislation, and his continued response was to say that drug prices will not rise as a result of his actions. That was about two years ago, and he has continued that argument in the months since then. In Ontario, the cost of a whole classification of drugs for elderly people, disabled people and singleincome families has doubled and tripled over the last several months as a result of the actions of this particular Minister. The title "Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs" is a misnomer, to say the least.
What is the Minister's argument in this case? He wants to improve services and cut costs, and in the process he will lay off something like 14 per cent of the workforce at Canada Post. If one says it quickly, it does not sound too bad: fourteen per cent of the workers. I want to tell Hon. Members what that means in real terms. We are talking about thousands of Canadian postal workers who will end up on the streets, at a time when many areas of Canada are facing totally unacceptable high rates of unemployment.
We are not talking only about postal workers and the impact on them and the reduction in services as a result of these layoffs but about their families, their friends and their neighbours. Many of these letter carriers have got to know the people they deliver mail to by name. What happens when we

lay these people off? The Government says that it is a costcutting move. Is it a cost-cutting move to throw someone out of a job and in the process slash services, necessary, essential services to Canadians?
There was a study done in the United States in the middle 1970s by the late Senator Humphrey. To my knowledge, there has not been a comparable study done in Canada. Senator Humphrey's study found that an increase in unemployment is associated with increases in other social problems like psychological problems, mental illnesses, wife battering and antisocial behaviour. The long-term effects of unemployment will not go away overnight when we restore full employment to the country, if that ever happens.
What about that postmaster in rural Canada who is laid off? In central Canada, and particularly in central and southern Ontario, we are not doing too badly right now. We are not doing as well as the Government would like us to believe we are doing, but we are not doing too badly. However, what happens in rural Canada? If a postmaster or postmistress is thrown out of work, he or she cannot walk across the street to find another job.
What happens to the person in Newfoundland, a letter carrier or an inside postal worker? In Newfoundland, there is an unemployment rate in the middle 20s. They simply cannot walk around and find other jobs. The same is true of those in the interior of B.C. and the Yukon. You cannot just walk across the street and find another job. There are thousands of people out of work in those communities. When the Government talks about improving the services and cutting costs, it has to consider the social implications of those actions. If it does not, it is being totally irresponsible. However, from what I have seen, that does not seem to matter.
Rather than cutting back on postal services, the Government should be expanding postal services. Why should Canada Post not only not run a deficit, why should it not make a profit? A sub-postmaster in Quebec asked why Canada Post does not do what other countries have done with their post offices. He says the new generation of postmasters might have an expanded role beyond providing traditional postal services. They could act as information agents for the federal Government on Manpower job-creation programs and serve as economic development agents as well. Rural post offices could easily generate more revenue by selling hunting and fishing licences, greeting cards and parcel wrapping materials in addition to accepting payment of utility bills. Over 2,000 small communities with post offices do not have banks, and banking is another service that could be provided following traditions in other jurisdictions.
I see my time is practically up so I just want to say that what we are seeing here in these actions taken by the Government has nothing to do with cost cutting and absolutely nothing to do with providing service to Canadians. We are
seeing an ideological approach to governing Canadians. The Government does not believe in providing service to average Canadians. As I said a minute ago, this issue will not disappear. People in rural Canada and in urban communities, people such as Residents Against Mailboxes and Rural Dignity, will not allow the Government to get away with what it is trying to do. I want to tell you that we in this Party are right behind them. We believe in fairness, equity, and that there are no second-class citizens in this country. Members opposite are going to pay for this in the next election.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my colleague how come in the past, when people wanted to settle somewhere, they would first look to see what services were available and then choose where to live, in view of the services they considered essential.
Today, people have the idea that they want to go to live somewhere and then they are surprised afterwards that all the services are not the same.
Could the Hon. Member explain to me how he sees this phenomenon in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, first, I think those Canadians who pay their fair share of taxes are entitled to exactly the same service as other Canadians who pay the same taxes. What the Hon. Member seems to be saying is something similar to what an official with Canada Post said to a spokesperson for Residents Against Mailboxes. That spokesperson said supermailboxes are creating tremendous problems for the disabled, particularly those confined to a wheelchair. You know what the Canada Post official said in response? Disabled people do not buy houses in these communities. Talk about stereotyping and discrimination against the disabled! Disabled people can buy houses just the same as other Canadians.
I do not buy that kind of argument at all. It is the same as what the Minister said to a question I asked in the House several weeks ago. I said to him that if he thinks these supermailboxes are the greatest thing since sliced bread, why not plunk one of these down on his own front lawn. "Be an example to the Canadians you are trying to convince", I said. He responded that his front lawn was a mess. He not only had a mailbox, he had a hydro pole, a fire hydrant and all kinds of things. In my mind that conjured up a visual mass of pollution in front of his house. In fact, I felt sorry for him. Then he said everybody should expect that in today's modern world, that you are not going to be able to live the way you did a 100 years ago.
I called a friend of mine who happens to live in Calgary and asked him to nip down to Harvie Andre's house and take a look at his front lawn. Maybe you can get a petition among the neighbours and force the city to clean it up for the poor guy. They went down and took a little peek at this guy's house. He
May 12, 1988

did not have a supermailbox there. Ele did not even have a mailbox. He did not even have a fire hydrant.
The Minister tends to exaggerate a little bit in trying to convince Canadians that we should accept the things the Government dictates. Canadians are not prepared to accept that, and I think every Canadian is entitled to equal service regardless of how the Government views it.

Mr. Speaker, in my constituency I have an area of old houses, very moderately priced. People who live there get door-to-door mail delivery. 1 also have areas with newer houses, much more expensive, running anywhere from $90,000 to $150,000. They pay higher income taxes than people in the older areas. They pay higher local taxes. They asked me why they cannot get the same door-to-door mail delivery as people in the older areas. They said to me that they did not accept as fact what the Government was imposing on them, that there are two classes of citizens. One class who get door-to-door delivery and another who does not.
I am wondering if the Hon. Member has heard the same complaint from people in his or other constituencies and whether he has an answer that is different from the one given by the Conservative Government and by the Liberals when they were the Government, that is, that we cannot afford it. Does he have an answer other than that which I could give to my constituents who are so angry despite the claims of the Post Office and the Minister that everyone is happy with the so-called supermailboxes?

Mr. Speaker, I have absolutely no idea why people cannot get equality of service, because it is something Canadians expect. I do not think any reasonable person in the country would argue that Canada Post should operate at a deficit. I certainly would not make that argument. However, I have also pointed out some programs and policies which Canada Post could enter into that could make it pay for itself. I sincerely believe that.
I heard the Minister arguing at one point that if we were to continue to provide that service it would mean an increase in postage rates equivalent to a 60-cent first-class stamp. I looked into that and found that, first, the Minister is talking about a set of circumstances that no one has been arguing. He would argue, and he is probably right in his estimate, that if door-to-door delivery were to be provided to every Canadian it would cost 60 cents for a first-class stamp. No one has ever argued for door-to-door delivery in areas where it never existed, such as in rural Canada.
When we break down his 60 cent figure according to our argument, the additional cost to extend services to those residents who are now serviced by supermailboxes and those who will be serviced by supermailboxes would be a maximum of some 2.3 cents, raising first class postage to about 41 cents or 42 cents. Therefore, I think there is a slight exaggeration.

It is the letter carriers' Alert Program where letter carriers keep an eye on elderly people. If they do not see someone during a certain period they would alert the necessary authorities that this elderly person may be in some difficulty.
I asked Canada Post officials what would happen to the letter carriers' Alert Program as a result of these supermailboxes being installed in these communities. They admitted that it would probably go by the way. That is extremely unfortunate.
People often criticize our postal workers for actions that are actually a policy of Canada Post. Yet, when workers themselves have instituted this program on a voluntary basis, I think it is a crying shame that the program, which has been of benefit to many seniors, will no longer be available. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested to hear the remarks of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) and the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young), and it is my firm opinion that the comments of his colleague from Winnipeg discriminate against Winnipeg customers.
Mr. Speaker, I think all Hon. Members, and especially the Hon. Member for Beaches, can rest assured that Canada Post did not shut down certain routes in this country just to deprive rural communities of postal services.
Perhaps I may recall the Corporation's objective, which is to work with communities to find other ways of increasing the number of outlets, to facilitate customer access to postal services, and to extend business hours by making use of the resources of local businesses and thus maintain and improve services.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may draw a comparison. When a bank closes down, the service it provides disappears along with it. When the Canada Post Corporation changed its postal services, it started offering a broader range of services. I would like to refer more specifically to a situation experienced by my mother, who gets her mail through the rural delivery service of Saint-Augustin. One day, Canada Post decided to ask people to drive nearly 10 kilometers to pick up their registered mail or items that were too big to fit in the little green box. Do you know what the people did, Mr. Speaker? They signed a petition and asked Canada Post to give them a service outlet at the local convenience store. Why? Because the convenience store was open from seven in the morning till midnight, provided good service and would obviate the need for driving 10 kilometers.
I think the lesson we can learn here, Mr. Speaker, is that when changes are made, the wishes of the community must be considered. In many cases, for instance in new developments, people have become used to going to the convenience store instead of doing their shopping on a larger scale. Habits have changed, and I think that is also reflected in the service offered by Canada Post.
Unlike what was said by the Hon. Member, and I was struck by this aspect as well, some municipalities in Quebec have adopted resolutions in which they ask super boxes because they feel this is an improvement. Every time I hear the Hon. Member talking about super mail boxes, it sounds like he is talking about a major disaster! You must not forget that some people, and some of them live in my riding, are very pleased and want the super mail boxes instead of the green boxes which are always falling down, aren't very clean and are not installed as a permanent fixture. Some people want the super mail boxes.
So I think that people who claim that super mail boxes represent a drop in service should remember that many people who are directly concerned see the boxes as an improvement.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to name the municipalities whose resolutions I have here: Saint-Luc, Sainte-Anne-de-Bellevue and Verdun. In each case, the municipality has advised Canada Post that this is an improvement in service and that people want the super mail boxes installed as soon as possible.
To recapitulate, Mr. Speaker, in some cases the super boxes mean an improvement in services, and it is also very important that Canada Post make these decisions with the community.
The same principle applies to everyone, and Canada Post must use its resources and skills to sell postal items and postal services. If we look at the present situation in Canada, we see that home delivery represents 54 per cent of postal services; centralized delivery, 13 per cent; super mail boxes and community mail boxes, 7 per cent; rural routes, 7 per cent; post office boxes, 15 per cent; and general delivery, 4 per cent.
When the population and the number of households increase, delivery networks must be expanded. If we look at what is happening in other countries, we see that many postal administrations, including the United States, Australia, France and Sweden, have concluded that universal home delivery is neither profitable nor affordable.
Here in Canada, home delivery would mean additional operating costs totalling $1.3 billion over five years and would oblige Canada Post to increase the basic letter rate by 17 cents, over and above any regular increases. That is why Canada Post is maintaining home delivery where it already exists and provides the super box service in new developments.
In rural areas, mail delivery has traditionally been carried out by local entrepreneurs. This delivery service is efficient and as profitable for Canada Post as it was previously for the Post Office. Local entrepreneurs are given a chance to participate
May 12, 1988

in postal service operations, while they remain free to conduct other business or to be otherwise employed.
Canada Post's objective, Mr. Speaker, consists in creating an efficient, modern and fully streamlined network of retail outlets that would improve access for customers, enhance Canada Post's image, provide a broader range of better quality and more regular services, and do so while making a profit.
Canada Post is trying to make its presence felt as an advanced enterprise in this country. A full range of postal products and services will be offered in the new network of postal outlets, which means that Canada Post will substantially increase the number of locations where retail services are offered, as well as upgrade the quality of those services.
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post expects to improve customer access by installing additional public mailboxes and super boxes where customers can both pick up and mail their letters. Another improvement will be to provide retail outlets in more convenient locations.
As far as mail delivery is concerned, Mr. Speaker, Canada Post has promised to maintain and improve the level of service provided to nearly 10 million addresses existing today. Elome delivery will be continued in locations where it now exists, while present routes will be expanded to include both sides of the street, up to the present cutoff point.
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post wants to give Canadians the assurance that new urban developments will continue to be served-and not later than 90 days after meeting all the usual criteria-by community mailboxes or super boxes.
Postal services to customers who now receive mail in community mailboxes or through general delivery will be improved through the installation of super boxes on an ongoing basis. In all, Mr. Speaker, some 340,000 rural and urban delivery points will be added to the superbox system over the next two years, and about 500,000 in three years, which should improve the present levels of service and accessibility.
Customers in cities where the population growth exceeds the capacity of the post office boxes at the local point of sale will have service at a super mailbox or community mail box.
In the year after Canada Post Corporation breaks even, it will adopt a policy of providing post office boxes free of charge for individuals whose only alternative is general delivery.
Rural route delivery service by private contractor will also be maintained.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must mention that Canada Post Corporation, which had a $600-million deficit in 1981, expects modest profits as of the 1988-89 fiscal year. It is also the first year that the Corporation will not ask for government subsidies to cover its expenses.
And, to use a well-known expression, Mr. Speaker, for once Canada Post will no longer be "in the red" starting this year.

Mr. Speaker, I have two questions I would like to pose to the Parliamentary Secretary. First, I would like to ask her to explain the discrepancy, as I understood her speech, between the 17 cents she talks about and the 60 cents the Minister has talked about in his wild and woolly way with respect to the differences in costs of basic service, first-class service, which would be required because of movement away from serving people with supermailboxes.
Second, and more important, I would like to challenge directly what the Member has suggested, that Canada Post is somehow committed to maintaining service door-to-door in every place it has existed. I can tell the Member that this is simply not the case and I can point specifically to sections of my constituency in which door-to-door delivery took place previously and which has now been cut out by Canada Post. If the Parliamentary Secretary wants the specific area, I can tell her it is along Highway 18, north of Amherstburg, an area which now has a condition in which half the area receives direct delivery and the other half, which is completely similar to the previous half, does not receive direct delivery. We had a situation prior to this Government taking office, and a situation prior to the changes which have taken place, in which everyone along that route received direct mail.
My last point is to say that there are small towns, urban areas, in effect, in my constituency which have every condition similar to that of the suburbs of the City of Windsor itself. Yet in the one set of conditions, they have door-to-door delivery, and in the other set of conditions, they do not have door-to-door delivery. There is an inequity here that is absolutely unacceptable to Canadians.
Does the Parliamentary Secretary not think that with the Charter of Rights setting forth the basic equalities which Canadians should have, it is quite likely there will be challenges by people who are faced with these inequalities, that they will directly challenge the policy that Canada Post, under the direction of this Government, has put into effect?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:

Regarding the maintenance of door-to-door services, with the example my colleague gave us from his own riding, I think

May 12, 1988

that I did say existing door-to-door service would continue. Service would be extended only if it were on the same street or for something that was already done, for example. For new developments, we will have to think of other ways to meet the public's demands.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is referring to a particular case of which I am not aware. Member is this: How can she explain that Canada Post management seem hellbent on systematically reducing services at a time when a small army of new companies is happily delivering mail?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano).

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part in this most important debate concerning the impact of Canada Post's decision to cut back on this vital and essential service to all Canadians.
We should realize nowadays that wherever we may go in this country, one of the main issues Canadians are concerned and wondering about is the postal service. I am sure that this is an issue which is certain to be raised during the forthcoming election.
This is so clear, Mr. Speaker, that as soon as Canada Post with its so-called responsible Minister learned this morning, or rather late last night, that we would deal today with an Opposition motion about postal services, it called a press conference to announce its action plan or annual report-we do not know which yet, but we will find out, I suppose, this afternoon-in an attempt to lead away from the real situation which we, as elected Members, will describe to Canadians during this allotted day.
First of all, I should like to start by saying that although on the one hand 1 was surprised to hear the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mrs. Tardif) (Charlesbourg) compare postal services to banking services, on the other hand it was not because, by comparing postal services to banking services, she provided us with the vary basic philosophy of the Tory party.
This is unbelievable, Mr. Speaker, in a country so large, so vast, and with such remote areas, as Canada! In a multicultural country! How vital must that postal service be! Some might say: hear now, when a bank decides to move a branch, nobody says anything, but when Canada Post Corporation decides to shut a post office down or move it, it becomes a problem.
May 12, 1988

This is exactly the point, Mr. Speaker. I believe this Conservative Government did not realize the importance of that service to Canadian communities, whether urban or rural. That service is a prime communications link, a highly important one, that we as a Government should be providing to Canadians.
When our Confederation was launched, Mr. Speaker, there were two major mandates: protecting and defending the country, and delivering the mail. But today we are wondering whether this Tory Government intends to continue. What we find is that with free trade, it intends to sell Canada out to the United States, and the experience with the postal service is clear evidence of that in my view.
Mr. Speaker, I should emphasize at this point that such is indeed Tory philosophy, and this is the reason why, in Canada Post's corporate plan tabled two years ago, it was clear that the Corporation was to shut rural post offices down, franchise urban offices and deliver mail to superboxes so that it could have it moved by contractors. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the Government's major goal was to privatize the postal service, and this is what it is trying to do by bits and pieces. But Canadians have caught on to that and it is my feeling that come the next election, we will hear about it, because it will be a highly debated issue and this Tory Government will get its answer.
Mr. Speaker, the other matter delved upon by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mrs. Tardif) is that some municipalities passed resolutions requesting that Canada Post Corporation install superboxes because installing them would improve service.
Mr. Speaker, what the Parliamentary Secretary did not say is that indeed there were cases where citizens said: We would rather have a mailbox than have to pick up our mail after work in a main post office, because closing hours often are a problem.
Clearly, when people have nothing, no mail at all, no mail delivery whatsoever, they will say: After all, if we have a box, it will be close to home. But that is not necessarily the kind of service they want, Mr. Speaker. If all Hon. Members would take the trouble to listen to their constituents, they would realize that whether they happen to be in urban or rural areas, people want the same postal services. Every day, town councils are adopting resolutions. You know what is happening? Spring is usually the time to start work on construction projects, and so Canada Post is getting into high gear with its supermailboxes. However, town councils have passed resolutions saying they don't want Canada Post to instal the boxes. Today, the Corporation is starting to play hardball: If you don't want supermailboxes in your municipality, we won't deliver the mail!
There will be no deliveries at all, and the people in your community will have to pick up the mail at a post office pretty far from where they live. That is the kind of pressure they are starting to put on local authorities who realize there are
Supply
Canadians who pay 37 cents to mail a letter, who pay the same municipal, provincial and federal taxes and that these people are entitled to the same services as everybody else. And that is the crux of the matter: the Government refuses to understand that delivering the mail to superboxes on a permanent basis, as announced, is discriminatory. Canadians will not accept it, and groups are getting organized across this country.
Not long ago, Mr. Speaker, I was in a Toronto suburb on a Sunday, at a meeting of some of these groups, including Residents Against Mailboxes, also known as RAM. Do you know what their slogan was?
"RAM the Mulroney box". That was their slogan. That is the kind of sentiment that is being generated these days. People are fed up with these supermailboxes. What they want is an efficient and fair mail service.
In rural areas, the Government intends to use collective mailboxes at major intersections. To my mind, this shows a lack of vision, a lack of understanding of the community fabric of Canada on the part of this Government. Everyone knows that the post office continues to be a gathering place in our villages and our small towns. It becomes an information centre for all citizens. It is where people go in search of information on the availability of social services; where they go to get taxation forms, scholarship forms, and job application forms. Often, the postmaster becomes a resource person.
Through the post office, the federal Government maintains a presence in our small towns and villages. Through the post office, the federal Government takes on human dimensions. It creates a link within the community, and it is a unifying force, a force which results in a feeling of belonging for members of the community.
To better express what I have been saying, let me quote from a letter which the Mayor of Trinity Bay, a small town, wrote to the President of the Canada Post Corporation. I quote:
If the few businesses which we have and on which we rely for our survival stay here, it is because we have services such as the post office. Centralization for economy's sake must not be pushed to such an extent that it jeopardizes the existence of small communities ... We urge you to find means to keep our post office, even if doing so would mean sharing with others certain of the most costly aspects of the postal service. For us here, sharing is a matter of survival, and we know something about it. For God's sake, do not help to destroy us!
Mr. Speaker, complaints are coming in from all over the country. Rural Dignity appeared before the Parliamentary Committee to describe the problem and explain how important it was to keep small post offices open in rural communities. We had citizens' groups like RAM appearing before the Committee to testify that supermailboxes are discriminatory. We even had test cases prove that homeowners living directly opposite

May 12, 1988
Supply
newly installed super boxes saw the value of their homes go down, and as a result, municipalities gave them a tax rebate.
Of course, we also had the whole issue of closing down some post offices and privatizing others. In my riding, for instance, I still get calls from people who live across from the post office and who received a card saying that from now on they would have to pick up their registered mail at the pharmacy on the other side of town. They now have to travel two miles by bus or on foot, depending on their budget, to pick up a parcel or a registered letter. That is what Canada Post and the Minister mean when they say they have improved services! In Saint-Leonard-Anjou, we now have five more locations where we can pick up the mail. Mr. Speaker, although this does mean that some people can pick up their mail at the pharmacy or the convenience store, what about the person who happened to buy a home near the post office and who could depend on that service, and now the service no longer exists?
Why do the Government and Canada Post not allow these people who are right near the post office to continue to pick up their mail and registered letters there? The reason is simple, Mr. Speaker: It is because Canada Post has decided, in its secret plan to privatize the Corporation, to gradually eliminate employees because there would be less volume and then to say four or five years later that there was not enough volume in those post offices and to shut them down. That is what is behind all that, Mr. Speaker, and I repeat, it is the plan to privatize Canada Post, to gradually shut down rural and urban post offices and to deliver the mail in supermailboxes in urban areas.
Of course, the Hon. Member for Vaileyfield, I think, would like me to shut my mouth! But I have the feeling that as soon as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has the courage to call an election, the citizens will really shut down the boxes and super mailboxes that the Conservative Government has set up, and as the RAM slogan goes, they will "ram the Mulroney mailboxes."
I think that this debate may be amusing for some Conservative Members, but it is important because some citizens across the country are concerned; they are disgusted and feel like second-class citizens. The Government is doing all this on the pretext of reducing the deficit. Well, Mr. Speaker, when Canada Post Corporation was created in 1981, with all three parties unanimously supporting the Bill, the new corporation had three objectives: namely, to improve service, reduce the deficit and improve labour relations. Today, the Conservative Government, after taking power, undid any improvement in labour relations that might have occurred from the time that Canada Post was created in 1981 until the Conservatives took power in 1984.
As for service, we know what that means: There are two classes of citizens, those who have home delivery and those who must get their mail from supermailboxes. The problem with this is that often you can see the mailman pass behind your house, through the yard, deliver mail to the neighbour,
and on the other side of the street, or one street over, you must get your mail from a supermailbox. If that is not discriminatory, I would like to know from the Conservative Government what is, and I hope that this afternoon, the Minister can tell us exactly in the House if it is not discriminatory, just what it is.
Definitely, Mr. Speaker, we must reduce the deficit. We agree on that. But we cannot reduce the deficit as fast as they want. In the United States, a country with 10 times our population and larger than ours, they took 14 years to balance the books. Here in Canada, they want to do it in seven years. And this has completely unbalanced the plans accepted in 1981, instead of letting things continue to reach our objective. In 1986, the Minister of Finance really burned his bridges and let us say that this is what has created the whole postal mess we find ourselves in today.
Of course there are ways to reduce the deficit, but not only by cutting expenses. We can also look for revenue. And how many times in this House and also in meetings outside have I suggested to the Minister and the Corporation how they could increase revenue!
On a parliamentary trip in Switzerland, I learned that they sell advertising space in their post offices, they sell public services such as public transit, for example, but they have advertising. Why would it not be possible for Canada Post Corporation, which owns some 4,000 trucks, to sell advertising space on its trucks, as buslines do? This would bring in revenues without entailing expenditures. Why could it not sell advertising space in post offices especially, of which there are a number downtown where people are ready to pay very good rates for advertising. The Corporation's answer to that is that such advertising would be detrimental to its image. Good gosh! What kind of an image is there when Canadians are mad and blowing their tops at the Corporation? I therefore feel that if we had a policy of using its buildings, trucks, and equipment to increase revenues instead of cutting down on service to people, this would be a boon.
There is also the whole matter of direct mail. There are very clear studies to show that we are eight years behind, that we could move forward in this area and get.. . Indeed, according to one study, if we did a per capita update on direct mail as they have done in the United States, we could get $300 million in extra income each year. This would be enough to wipe out the deficit, have home delivery in urban areas and keep our post offices in rural areas.
This is a matter let us say of good will, but as suggested by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, this Government has decided to compare Canada Post Corporation, the postal service, to a banking service.
This means that a bank, as any other business, plans its operations and must gererate a profit at years's end. If the operation is not profitable, they either shut the branch down or move it elsewhere.
May 12, 1988

But such is not the case. The postal service is a basic communication service for Canadians. And in a country as large, as vast and diversified as Canada we must have the same postal service for all. We are going to fight to make the postal issue a priority during the next elections, Mr. Speaker, and Canadians will judge this Tory Government accordingly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to return to my hon. friend's last statement to the effect that I compared Canada Post services to banking services. That is not quite what I said, Mr. Speaker. I said that after a bank closes, banking services are no longer provided. On the other hand, when Canada Post decides for instance to close a post office somewhere, it makes sure that somebody else will provide the service. This is altogether different, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to return also to another statement made by my hon. friend. He referred earlier to the objectives the former Liberal government was attempting to reach when postal services became the responsibility of Canada Post Corporation and no longer of a government department.
As far as I can remember, the previous Government decided to make the Post Office department into a so-called "independent" Crown Corporation so that postal services provided to Canadians would be free of political interference.
If that was the purpose then as well as to make sure that Canada Post was free to provide Canadians with services which could be financed by raising funds through the sales of stamps and services, I wonder what my hon. friend would say for instance in the case of collective bargaining when one must appear before a mediator to express his or her views or those of a group of unionized workers. When a Member of Parliament speaks out in favour of unionized workers before a mediator should this be considered as political interference? Does this mean that, depending on the situation, the Liberals with their global view of things could argue: "Our objective is to avoid political interference; just the same, when dealing with day by day issues, interference is sometimes necessary".
Is it more important to make sure that Canadians as a whole get postal services? As I said earlier, we are not trying to reduce postal services, only seeking different ways to provide them.
When you mentioned reduced services, is it because you felt that Canada Post employees are not good employees, that they are not providing Canadians with the services they should? This seems to be the gist of your remarks.
I can tell you, for sure, and I know a number of Canada Post employees, that most of them are good employees anxious to provide their customers with the services they have the right to expect.

Precisely, Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary is telling us that nobody should interfere with the mandate of Canada Post which was created in this House in
Supply
1981 by a Liberal Government with the unanimous support of all Members.
As it happened, when the Conservative Government took over it did intervene and did interfere with this clear-cut threepronged mandate: Better services, improved labour relations, and deficit reduction. Those were the three objectives of Canada Post. It was this Conservative Government-her Government, Mr. Speaker-which chose to interfere and completely alter the course we had plotted for Canada Post. With their new plan to shut down 5,000 rural post offices, install superboxes in urban centres and city outskirts, not to mention franchising and closing post offices in urban areas, that is when the whole debate on Canada Post was re-opened, precisely because the Conservative Government had interfered and got mixed in Canada Post operations to say: No, from here on in this is how you are going to operate.
It was the Government which interfered, not the Opposition.
As to the mediator... I was laughing earlier because I see that the Parliamentary Secretary is remotely controlled by Canada Post, and this spirit, the attitude which now prevails in the upper reaches of Canada Post, Mr. Speaker, and indeed any action that might be taken ... I want my colleague to have a copy of the presentation I made before the mediator. She will see that it is a complete presentation on the way we could have broken the deadlock.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the conclusion of my presentation. I said to the mediator: Of course, both parties are to blame. So I was not siding with the employees. I even explained how to increase revenues, what labour relations approach to take to settle the whole dispute. Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that in the space of six months... There were no strikes between 1981 and 1987. In a six month period in 1987, we had two strikes for which this Tory Government was responsible. The Corporation could erupt like a volcano any 2 minute. This is precisely the attitude which I note in the comment made by the Parliamentary Secretary under the guidance of Canada Post Corporation when she stated that I appeared before the mediator to plead on behalf the union. I did not defend the union, Mr. Speaker. I said to the mediator that definitely all the blame was not to be laid on the same side. There has been abuse everywhere in that organization precisely because labour relations are in such a sorry state.
Therefore I said to the mediator: Sir, I feel that your work is extremely valuable. Your recommendations will have a direct and permanent effect on our postal service. I cannot overly insist on the necessity of maintaining for Canadians a fair and efficient postal service which will take into account the nature of this country as well as budgetary constraints. We should return to our three great principles, which are to harmonize labour relations, to improve service and reduce the deficit. Such were the basic principles when Canada Post Corporation was set up. If there is interference with the business of Canada Post, it is precisely that of the Conservative Government and

May 12, 1988
Supply
its action plan. And we will see if the plan they put forward this afternoon is better or worse.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Richmond- Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) for a question or comment.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief comment and ask a question. As for the comment, somebody mentioned the banks and I think indeed there is an interesting parallel to draw here. As far as I know, in rural areas as in my constituency, there are relatively few banks.
However, there are Caisses populaires everywhere, even in the smallest communities. And, to my knowledge, in spite of the small number of people they serve, the Caisses populaires are very profitable because they were able to adjust, to tailor their services to people's needs.
As for my question, I would like first to congratulate my colleague. The Government seems to consider Canada Post merely as a private enterprise having to act and to face the same obligations as a private company. But, to me, there is a big difference between Canada Post and a private company, given its purpose and its unifying role.
My question to my colleague is this: How does he see Canada Post in relation to private enterprise?

Of course, Mr. Speaker, if Canada Post is to be considered as a private enterprise, I admit it would be easy to privatize it if the Government were to decide overnight to sell postal services in Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver and in every large city, then of course it could make good use of the money.
But what happens when you have to provide postal services to rural areas, to the North, to our remote areas? As I was saying in my speech it is important that the Government take a good look at Canada Post as everybody was unanimously prepared to do in 1981, and give it specific objectives. It should have been allowed to continue, and perhaps today we would not have a deficit but instead an improved and equitable service for all Canadians.
So, Canada Post cannot be considered as a private enterprise. Even in the Marchment Report, in the section on privatization, they make this comparison. They say that for large cities it would be easy to privatize, but who would pay for services elsewhere? Would the private enterprise be ready to pay the costs of shipping a letter to remote areas? That is what the universality of the system is all about. We pay 37 cents to send a letter to Ottawa or Toronto but also to Yellowknife. So you can be sure that if Canada Post were a private enterprise, with the deregulation system that is being pushed too far, Canadians living in remote areas, in the North for example, could not get any service.
So that is why we want to balance the books and take the time needed, but also we want to give Canadians the service they are entitled to get.
Mrs.Tardif (Charlesbourg): Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. colleague why when comparing Canada Post and the private sector, he distinguishes between their customer service? When we talk about 37 cents postage it means whether the letter is sent to the same town or to the Far North, I think everyone agrees with this. This is one of the aims of Canada Post Corporation. It is precisely the reason why it is not a private company. On the other hand, one of its mandates was to operate on a balanced budget. There has never been any question that service to the people should not cost the same everywhere. We know full well that when we talk about new service expansion, Canada Post is of the opinion that in the years to come, the type of new project development will have to change.
Is it not the same for many other services? I am thinking of people who, in the old days, did their shopping at one main grocery store. Today, they stop every evening at the convenience store. Is it not also true that our way of life has changed in such a way that our habits have changed and one of the way Canada Post Corporation can meet the expectations of its customers is also to adapt to the new ways of a new generation.

Mr. Speaker, of course we all agree on paying 37 cents, no matter where we live in Canada. However, if you pay the same amount, you expect to get the same level of service as other Canadians.
But things work differently. For instance, in my riding, on a street not far from mine, people living on one side of the street get their mail delivered, others do not. Thus the postman delivers mail to citizens like myself living on one side of the street, whereas people who live just accross the street, in the new developments built in the Spring of 1985, must get theirs from a mailbox. Canadians find this unacceptable. Why this double standard on the same street?
As for the comparison between supermarkets and corner stores, I have to say that when we, Liberals, were in power, we opened postal branches and counters in drugstores. We did that to accomodate people, the same way corner stores do, so that people requiring immediately different postal services could get them right away without having to go to the main post office. But the main post office did, however, exist.
What is happening now is that with its new scheme, Canada Post is taking a postal branch that provides complete services in a drugstore or a convenience store, and franchising it. Those are the reasons why the plan does not work. Canadians are not willing to accept it. In that sense, Mr. Speaker, practically everybody living in a rural area is against it today. People are protesting because their small post office is closing down. For their part, city dwellers are critical because they must go to supermailboxes to get their mail. Furthermore, customers who need postal services are not satisfied to go to these franchised post offices. Therefore, a monster has been created which upsets everybody.
May 12, 1988

Mr. Speaker, we in the Opposition are not the only ones to condemn the Government for its total and absolute failure to provide fair and equitable postal service to all Canadians. We are joined by a majority of Canadians who feel they were victims of the cutbacks by Canada Post, or had seen their neighbours or friends or parts of their communities affected by these government-ordered cut-backs. Even organizations such as the Catholic Bishops have stressed the need to provide services in communities where those services are an integral part of the survival of those communities. The United Church of Canada agreed and gave its support to the people trying to maintain the postal service at the level we are used to.
The Minister responsible for Canada Post keeps trying to convince us that there is no reduction in service. The statements he makes are a patent attempt to create a false image. This has made many people angry in the sense they feel that the Minister is being condescending towards them. It has affected the credibility of all the Minister's statements. In fact, it affects the credibility of the Government to a great extent because it knows services have been cut back. The Government knows fewer services are being provided now than in the past. It knows the service being provided in one part of the country or a community is not the same as that provided in a different part or community, even if conditions are exactly the same.
Everyone who lives anywhere near a post office which has been closed during the last three or four years knows that service has been taken away. Everyone who no longer has a rural route delivery knows there has been a reduction in service. When we say, as we do in this resolution, that we condemn the Government for its total and absolute failure to provide fair and equitable postal service to all Canadians, we are just representing people who have felt the reduction in service.
When the Minister says he has not reduced service, he is obviously talking through his hat because 200 rural post offices have been closed. Dozens of rural routes have been eliminated wherever possible. The Minister states that service is not being reduced, so that means he is giving a wrong impression and stretching credibility.
My special concern here today is that of reduction in rural service. We need to think about what rural life really is. What is the reality? Perhaps the Minister who defends Canada Post's actions to such a great extent should be given a course on rural reality. It might be more valuable to him than his Ph.D. In his attempts to defend the postal service he seems not to recognize that there is a special quality to rural life which must be recognized and nurtured to some extent. There is a rural infrastructure which we should build on. It provides the kind of lifestyle which many of our people are considering more and more important to the well-being of the country. A
Supply
vibrant and viable rural community has built into it a range of services which are necessary to its survival and growth.
Rural communities are not just people who live on the farm. Rural communities include small towns, villages and hamlets. It is a combination of producers and consumers. To survive, a rural community must be self-sufficient within certain parameters. One of those parameters is the requirement for postal services. Certain communities cannot survive without certain services being available, and one of those services is postal service.
A removal of the postal service is almost a death sentence for a particular community. What are the realities of a rural post office? First, it is vital to the economic and social wellbeing of the community. It is the only federal presence in the community. Quite often a general store, a gas station or a post office are the centre of village life. If you remove the post office, you have removed one-third of the commercial presence of many small villages. You then move towards the elimination of that village entirely. If the people of a particular community are forced to go eight, 10 or 15 miles to another community down the road to get their mail, they very quickly start to do other business in that community and consequently their own village may well disappear.
Seniors in particular are seriously affected by changes in postal service. Many do not have cars to drive to the next nearest post office. They have to choose between increasing dependency on other people or isolation. They also find themselves in a very difficult situation if they are forced to go to supermailboxes which are quite often beside or along busy streets or highways. They do not have the kind of protection they are used to in their small local post office.
Women constitute about 82 per cent of Canada's rural postmasters and their assistants, so that elimination of those post offices eliminates many jobs for women. Closing a post office in many cases removes the only jobs available to rural women in a given area. Yet quite often that reduces the amount of service to the area. Furthermore, a store owner will give priority to someone buying groceries over someone coming to buy a 37 cent stamp.
Privatization of the post office also results in the postmaster and their assistants receiving one-fifth the salary they received previously, which also reduces the economic effect of the post office on that community.
The Minister has tried to convince us that there has been no change in service. Recently I gave him an opportunity to make an honest man of himself by opening up the 200 post offices that have been closed in the last two years, including a number of rural post offices.
My own rural delivery has been closed and I now drive 20 miles, twice a week, to get my mail, when I used to get it across the road from the farm. There are 35 other farm

May 12, 1988
families in the same situation. That has to be considered a reduction in service.
In the last two years, 37 post offices have been closed in Saskatchewan. That number has probably increased significantly in the last few weeks because there is a meeting today in the small town of Pilger in an attempt to save the post office. Yesterday there was a meeting in the small town of St. Gregor, not far from Humboldt, where the postmaster is retiring and Canada Post is attempting to close the post office. 1 believe they have reached a compromise in that case.
The town of Clavet, situated close to Saskatoon, is also affected by this change in the post office. These changes are supposed to be improvements, according to the Minister, but in the minds of the people in the communities they represent a withdrawal of service.
The committee which dealt with this issue faced some difficulties. The committee, which was dominated by Conservative Members, refused to hear several witnesses who wanted to indicate their displeasure with the corporate plan that had been established by the post office. In its final report, even Conservative Members said that there should be no closure without meaningful consultation and the consent of the community affected, and that the retirement of a postmaster should not in itself constitute a criterion for closing rural post offices.
Unfortunately, these two recommendations, while accepted by the Post Office, have not been fulfilled.
Recently, there was a much publicized case in Saskatchewan where the sudden death of the postmaster was used as an opportunity by Canada Post to close the post office. It is rather difficult to give 90 days' notice in these circumstances. The post office has been moved to the local grain elevator. One can imagine where the priority will lie if someone comes to buy grain and another person comes to buy a 37 cent stamp.
Since 1986, post offices have been closed in almost every part of the country. The post office in Purple Springs, Alberta, closed on July 31, 1986. Those residents must drive 34 kilometres return to pick up their mail at Taber. The mail truck continues to pass through the small town of Purple Springs on its way to deliver the mail at Taber.
The post office in Ninga, Manitoba, was closed on August 1, 1986, forcing residents to make a 35 kilometre round trip to pick up their mail. Residents in Ravenscrag, Saskatchewan, must travel 80 kilometres return to Eastend to pick up their mail and conduct postal business.
The corporate plan that was presented by the Government in 1986 stated: "We have 5,221 rural post offices in Canada. Over the next 10 years, 1,700 smaller post offices are to be closed and replaced by supermailboxes". It goes on to say that 3,500 post offices are to be privatized. The post office would be closed, and retail services would be provided in a local grocery store, drug store and so on.
In response to this plan it was stated that employees would not be properly trained by experienced, sworn-in postmasters but by poorly paid store clerks with a high turnover rate.
This action by the Government constitutes a major change for people in these communities. We must recognize the need for the continuity of rural Canada which the removal of postal services does not provide. In many cases, the survival of the community is dependent upon the existence of the service.
When the Government moved against rural post offices in Canada, it moved against residents of rural Canada. The vision of Rural Dignity, an organization that was established to protect as many of these rural post offices as possible, represents a vision of a proud people who believe they are contributing to Canada. Recognition of that contribution can be made by allowing these people the best possible service, including postal service.
The downgrading of rural Canada is a contribution to the depopulation of rural Canada. In Saskatchewan, post offices have been closed in the communities of Aylesbury, Esk, Krydor, Elstow, Readlyn, Forgan, Tweedsmuir, and Crutwell. All of these communities feel they have been attacked by the Government. They want to fight back by requesting the continuity of their rural post offices.

May 12, 1988

the road on the Ottawa River Parkway, while cyclists and runners will be using the other side.
An RCMP spokesman said about this new policy: "We're kind of crossing our fingers", obviously meaning that hopefully the regular users of the Parkway on Sunday morning will not be featured in Monday morning's obituaries. speakeroldname: Mrs. Shirley Martin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
maintopic: WINONA HIGH SCHOOL STUDENTS-TELETHON CHARITY DRIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the youth of Canada are our hope and inspiration for the future. They often demonstrate their beliefs and concerns for our nation by becoming involved in a project that will benefit their community. The students of Winona High School in Lincoln riding are an excellent example of Canadian youth working together for the benefit of their community.
May 14 will be Winona High's thirteenth telethon since 1974. In previous years the school has raised over $150,000 for charitable organizations such as the Multiple Sclerosis Society, Participation House, the Winona Senior Citizens Centre, and the Spinal Cord Society.
This concern for and commitment to the community demonstrated by hundreds of Winona students have earned for them the affectionate title of "The Small School with the Big Heart". Although this is Winona High School's farewell telethon, the spirit of Winona High will live on in the hearts of the students, the teachers, and the hundreds of citizens whom the youth of Winona High have helped through their telethons.

Mr. Speaker, today being International Nurses Day and the birthday of
Florence Nightingale who pioneered nursing, I ask Members to join with me in paying tribute to Canada's dedicated and caring nurses.
Nurses play a vital role within the health care system. Not only do they care for those of us who are sick but they provide pre-natal and post-natal clinics for new mothers, preventive health care in schools and in communities, and important support services which allow elderly and disabled people to remain independent in their communities.
I would also like to give special recognition to Jeanne Mance who was Canada's first nurse and hospital administrator. She established the first hospital in New France. Her belief in preventive health care showed remarkable foresight. She recognized that the maintenance of health and prevention of illness should be the most important goal of our health care system.
In Ottawa this evening the Canadian Nurses Association will hold a media awards dinner to recognize journalists from across Canada for their excellence in health reporting. The National Federation of Nurses' Unions has organized fund raisers. We are indeed fortunate that nurses care.

maintopic: S. O. 21 YOUTH YES CANADA-OU1 CANADA
S. O. 21 YOUTH YES CANADA-OU1 CANADA
speechtext:
There are many organizations in Canada which give assistance to the 434,000 young unemployed across the country. YES Canada is one of them.
This dynamic organization helps young dropouts complete their basic training and provides them with the tools they need in order to meet the numerous challenges they face.
YES Canada will complete its pilot project in December 1988. The results to date speak for themselves: 78 per cent of young people who took part in the program have found a steady job or have gone back to school.
The Government should not only support this humanitarian project, but also allocate the necessary funding so that the program can be offered in French and gain national status. A bilingual program would be accessible to all young Canadians who urgently need support.
Will the Conservative Government take action to show that it is concerned with the situation of all young people in Canada by allocating funds so that young French Canadians can take advantage of a commendable project like YES Canada?
The Conservative Government tends to forget that all begins with youth and that young people are our most reliable resource.

Mr. Speaker, Focus on Inputs is an association representing about 3,500 prairie farmers. This group is dedicated to providing practical economic benefits to farmers through research into generic herbicides.
The present process for registration of farm chemicals is an expensive and complex one. This process effectively produces a barrier to entry into the chemical manufacturing market. Prairie farmers faced with rising input costs and depressed grain prices are seeking ways to help themselves out of the present situation.
By seeking to have pesticide requirements modified to suit the interests of farmers better, Focus on Inputs is attempting to put farmers in a position to create a better future.
Including farm chemicals under Section 41 of the Patent Act would also be beneficial to our farmers. Farm chemicals
could be treated in much the same manner as pharmaceutical drugs by the Patent Act through the introduction of compulsory licensing. This would allow the production of generic herbicides 10 years after a product was first registered. In return, the generic manufacturer would pay a 14 per cent royalty on sales until the original company's 17-year patent expires.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, improvements in this area are necessary in order to reduce input costs for Canadian farmers.

FUNDING OF WELFARE SERVICES FOR CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several years ago an agreement was arrived at between the federal Department of Indian Affairs, the Manitoba Department of Community Services, and the Indian Child Welfare Agencies, under which the agencies took over the delivery of child welfare services for native children. It was agreed by Indian Affairs that the level of services provided for native children would be equal to the standard provided by the non-Indian agencies in Manitoba to other children.
However, the Department of Indian Affairs has refused to increase the funding required to provide those services, the cost of which has gone up substantially since the agreement was arrived at. I call on the Department of Indian Affairs to honour its agreement so that Indian children in need can get the same consideration as all other children in need in Manitoba.

subtopic: CLOSURE OF MUNICIPAL INCINERATOR IN METROPOLITAN TORONTO
CLOSURE OF MUNICIPAL INCINERATOR IN METROPOLITAN TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, May 10, the Council of Metropolitan Toronto took strong action for clean air and conservation by voting to close the Commissioners Street municipal incinerator on July 1 next.
Reports of the Environmental Protection Office of the Toronto Board of Health show that unacceptable quantities of dioxins and heavy metals from the incinerator are fouling the air Torontonians breathe.
After a campaign by groups such as Citizens for a Safe Environment, CUPE Local 43, including the garbage collectors, and the New Democratic City Hall Caucus, Toronto Council voted unanimously to close the incinerator, and Metro Council agreed by a majority.
The Citizens for a Safe Environment group now proposes that the 70 incinerator staff be re-employed at reducing waste destined for landfill by, (1) organizing reduction of industrial waste at source; (2) resale of usable waste-for example, wood-to appropriate users; and (3) recycling glass, for example, into new products.
Toronto has given a good lead, and I hope other cities will follow that lead.

Mr. Speaker, the assumption in our tax laws and public policy is that one is either a farmer or one is not. However, testimony given by the Canadian Cattlemen's Association to the Senate Committee on Agriculture suggests that, in future, two different types of agriculture will emerge.
On the one hand there will be the sophisticated, large, capital-intensive agri-business operations; on the other, there will be smaller operations, owned and managed by people with

May 12, 1988
off-farm employment. In the future, most of the rural population will have a job, either full or part-time, as well as being farmers.
We should recognize this trend and, in our future policies, make due allowance for the fact that, in the coming years, most smaller farmers will be engaged in farming on a parttime basis, deriving much of their income from non-farm activities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last election campaign, this Tory Government made all sorts of promises to Canadian senior citizens. Everybody remembers their promise to fully indexed old age pensions. They broke their word and tried to cut old age security pension payments.
They undertook to expand the New Horizons Program to meet the needs of senior citizens in golden age clubs. But once again, they reneged on their promise and reduced funding.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that none of the Canadian senior citizens listening to us will want to vote for a Tory candidate because that party doesn't keep its promises.

Mr. Speaker, for over 300 years, competent and dedicated nurses have looked after Canadian men and women in Canada. The fact that Canada has over 200 000 active nurses, representing more than 50 per cent of the total number of health care professionals, is a good indication of the importance of that profession within our national health care system.

On behalf of all Canadian men and women and in recognition of their contribution to the public health and welfare, I remind Members of Parliament and the Canadian people that May 9th is the National Nurses Week in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the state of housing for Indian people is a disgrace. Forty per cent of Indian housing units do not have access to running water or bathing facilities, as opposed to 1 per cent of housing units across Canada. The Government's innovative solution seems to be to provide housing that no one can afford.
As of April 1, 1988, a number of band members in my riding received notices that their rents would be increased by anywhere from 50 per cent to 100 per cent. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if this happened in Toronto there would be a riot.
In my riding people have moved out of this housing and are planning to live in tents for the summer because they cannot afford the increases. Bands are left with having to make payments on units for which they receive no revenue. The Department of Indian Affairs and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation have implemented a program which is not helping those the program was intended to help.
I call on the Government to place an immediate freeze on these totally unacceptable rent increases and to review completely the entire scheme with the bands involved.

CHALLENGE '88 MOUNT ROYAL RIDING-APPLICATION APPROVAL RATE

May 12, 1988

One has only to look around my riding to see students looking for work who should have been better served by the Government if this Government had had a strong commitment to youth and summer jobs, jobs which give students money and the valuable career experience they need.
The Government promised jobs, jobs, jobs. Well, all we have seen are cuts, cuts, cuts. Another broken Tory promise.

Mr. Speaker, Lucien Bouchard, the Minister or messiah who was going to rescue the Conservative Party from electoral failure was also supposed to make recommendations to the Prime Minister concerning ethical standards, conflicts of interest, and cleaning up election expenses.
