subsubtopic: PENSIONS FOR WOMEN HOMEMAKERS-REQUEST THAT MINISTER REVEAL PROVINCES' DISAGREEMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while the Conservative Government is muddying the reputation of all Members in this House, there are people in need, and my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The Minister admitted yesterday that during the course of this session the Conservative Government could not honour its commitment to introduce the homemakers' pension under the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan because it could not get provincial agreement. Can the Minister indicate the reasons expressed by dissenting provinces for opposing the homemakers' pension?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: PENSIONS FOR WOMEN HOMEMAKERS-REQUEST THAT MINISTER REVEAL PROVINCES' DISAGREEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member stated in the preamble to his question that we were not going to fulfil our obligations. That is not correct. In fact yesterday in the House I quoted directly from our policy handbook. I do so again: "We encourage the provinces to agree to the introduction of a homemakers pension in the Canada Pension Plan, along the lines proposed by the Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform".
Furthermore, in discussions with the provinces on changes to the Canada Pension Plan, in 1985 a proposal to include the homemakers in the Canada Pension Plan along the lines proposed by the Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform was put to the provinces.
I also remind the Hon. Member that, following that, a report on the viability of a homemaker's pension in the Canada Pension Plan was commissioned. He should be aware of that report. I understand that it has been completed but I do not yet have it in my hands. Obviously I look forward to seeing its recommendations and how we can go beyond the proposals that we made in the campaign of 1984.

May 12, 1988
Oral Questions

subtopic: QUERY CONCERNING PROVINCES OPPOSED TO PROJECT

May we know which provincial governments are delaying such an important plan to introduce a homemakers' pension?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. It concerns the opening of this ministerial office/campaign office in Alma
in the riding of Lac-Saint-Jean where a by-election is being held on June 20.
Recently Canadians responded to many polls across the country that they consider integrity and ethics as the key elements on which they judge politicians and political leaders. speechtext:

Surely an office in an area where he will be occupied for the next two months is clearly realistic, reasonable, and feasible. Certainly in the discharge of that responsibility Canadians would want to separate political campaign activity from legitimate government departmental business activity. I think that is what is happening in this particular case.

In the eyes of the New Democratic Party. subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ALLEGED VIOLATIONS OF POLLUTION LAWS BY PULP MILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of the Environment and of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The West Coast Environmental Law Association reports that 21 of 22 pulp mills in British Columbia consistently violated federal pollution laws last year without being charged. Why did the Government of Canada allow such poor application of the law? What is the Government going to do to enforce existing federal pollution laws to protect the environment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ALLEGED VIOLATIONS OF POLLUTION LAWS BY PULP MILLS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will take the question as notice. I can only indicate to the Hon. Member that there is an outstanding issue relating to access to information which is due shortly and which I believe will cover that issue even more fully.

subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ALLEGED VIOLATIONS OF POLLUTION LAWS BY PULP MILLS
speechtext: We don't need access to information data to find out what is happening every day. The record for 1987 is matched by an even more miserable record in 1985 and 1986. We don't need any reference to the Information Act.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think Members know very fully that the Minister of the Environment has been very active dealing with effluents from pulp mills, whether one is dealing with dioxins or fluorines. I think as well the Member, who was a former Minister of the Environment, would want to congratulate the present Minister who was awarded a very prestigious award in the United States by the Sierra Club for his work on the environment. I am sure the Hon. Member would want to congratulate his successor for receiving an award which he himself never received.
I am sure as well that the Hon. Member would want to take cognizance of the fact that the Environmental Protection Act has passed third reading. It is an Act which he was never able to get through the House, but the present Minister has. I hope the Liberal Senate will approve it as well. Those are the kinds of positive actions the Minister of the Environment has taken. Regrettably, some of those actions were not taken earlier by the questioner.

speechtext:

... take all possible measures within the limits of its constitutional
authority to prohibit the export of Canadian water by interbasin diversions;

subtopic: PRAIRIE DROUGHT CONDITIONS-STUDY OF POSSIBLE WATER DIVERSION TO NORTH DAKOTA
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. It deals with the Government's failure to introduce legislation restricting advertising of tobacco products. Is it not really the free trade deal that is causing the stall on Bill C-51?

No, Mr. Speaker, the free trade deal has nothing to do with Bill C-51 as the Deputy Prime Minister and other House officers have indicated. Health Organization on tobacco consumption, of approximately 166 countries Canada was either eighth or ninth highest in the world.

subsubtopic: WHEREABOUTS OF ALLEGED KILLER OF CANADIAN SOLDIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice who is aware that Wilhelm Mohnke has been located in Hamburg, West Germany. This individual was on Canada's most wanted war criminal list following World War II, alleged to have killed 52 Canadian soldiers who were prisoners of war after the Normandy invasion. The West German Government has indicated it is not planning to conduct any more investigations, or to prosecute this individual.
In light of the fact that the Canadian Government has collected its own evidence on the subject I want to ask the
Oral Questions
Minister whether he is prepared to get in touch with West German authorities to urge them to accept our evidence to complete this investigation, and to lay charges.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):

subsubtopic: WHEREABOUTS OF ALLEGED KILLER OF CANADIAN SOLDIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will understand as a former Solicitor General that it would be improper for me to comment on investigations that I am making with respect to criminal charges. He can rest assured, in any case, that the Government of Canada stands ready to co-operate with respect to prosecutions or investigations that may be undertaken. I can give the Hon. Member that assurance.
We are prepared to co-operate. Indeed, the Hon. Member has written to me, and I have responded to him, to give him that assurance. If he has any information that would be useful, I wish that he would turn that information over to my Department.

speechtext:

I want to ask the Minister again at least to undertake to review the material that is there, and to make representations to the West German Government urging it to change its decision, and to lay charges.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER URGE WEST GERMAN GOVERNMENT TO LAY CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I reiterate and give the Hon. Member the commitment with respect to any information that is turned over, or any investigation, that clearly we will co-operate in order that the interests of justice are in fact achieved. I do not think the Hon. Member wants me to comment with respect to information that we might have in our investigation.
The Hon. Member wrote to me. I have, as a result of his letter, communicated with the British Labour Member of Parliament to whom he referred with respect to information. I have asked my Department to be in communication with him to see if there is any additional information that he can bring forward.
I simply say to the Hon. Member that in our system of justice we do not make public details of the extent of our investigations that are taking place, except to say this, that as Attorney General I can assure the Hon. Member that where there is a legitimate case, a serious and credible situation, and there is evidence, we will be co-operating with other countries, or dealing with the matter in our own jurisdiction.

subsubtopic: NON PAYMENT OF TAX BY CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of State for Finance.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance was asked to explain how it is that, despite his tax reform program, more than 5,000 high income Canadians paid no income tax at all last year, and he defended the situation by saying that the numbers had been reduced substantially since the Government took office.
I would ask the Minister of State for Finance to explain how it is that, despite tax reform, a number of the largest corporations in Canada, corporations which made substantial profits, in fact paid no income tax at all in 1986.
Alcan Aluminum, with profits of $306 million, paid no corporation tax; Brascan, with profits of $186 million, paid no corporation taxes; Power Financial, with profits of $131 million, paid no corporation taxes; Hees International, with profits of $117 million, paid no corporation tax.
Indeed, most were able to accumulate tax credits for future use.

subsubtopic: NON PAYMENT OF TAX BY CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the Hon. Member's question is that tax
Business of the House
reform came into effect in 1987 and not in the year to which the figures that the Hon. Member has quoted apply.

Mr. Speaker, does the Minister not realize that the reason these corporations paid no taxes and that nothing has changed is that they were able to defer the taxes that they should have paid, and that in fact those deferred taxes will never be paid?
Given that these corporations will continue to build new buildings and acquire new equipment, those deferred taxes will never be paid, with the result that these corporations will pay no corporation tax at all.
When is the Government going to plug those loopholes?

Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that this Tory Government has adopted toward this issue an offhand attitude which is altogether unacceptable.

A second report was recently tabled which contains some very interesting elements. The committee was happy to say that its report was unanimous. It is saving a few thousand dollars thinking that that will be enough to cover a deficit of hundreds of millions of dollars.
So, I think that it was absolutely realistic and reasonnable that the committee came to such a unanimous conclusion.
This report also states "that the Committee regrets the heavy-handed way Canada Post has gone about shutting down certain post offices and wishes that in the future a minimum 90 days' notice be given before closing a post office to allow for consultation with the people concerned." And the Committee's findings and recommendations are as follows: That no rural post office be closed and that no postal service be altered without prior consultation with an approval by the community involved; that the period of consultation be at least 90 days; that Canada Post corporation immediately inform a Member of Parliament when shut-downs or changes are proposed in their ridings; that local officials be also consulted; that, during consultations, not only the changes proposed by the Corporation but also the alternative be closely examined; finally, that a postmaster's departure or retirement not be the sole criterion for shutting down a rural post office or for altering postal services.

In my riding, for instance, there is a large community called Saint-Framjois, where the people learned one morning, out of the blue, that Canada Post Corporation was not going to renew the postmaster's mandate and that, to get the services provided up to now by the post office, they would have to go to a grocery store.
Of course, there was a flood of protest. My feeling was that 1 should go and consult the people who were particularly affected by this policy change. I sent a personal letter to every member of the community in this village, asking for their comments. I must say- and the results of my survey were positive-that a little more than half of the people saw a number of positive elements in this policy. They said for instance: from now on, the post office will be open longer for us to pick up the mail.
When Canada Post realized I was doing this survey, a month later it decided to do its own consultation. This proves that the whole exercise was rather haphazard. Obviously, Canada Post could have used a survey to involve the community in this decision and thus avoid the spate of criticism, disagreement and confusion. In any case, a number of people protested vehemently against the post office closings and I will
tell you what their comments were. I must say I found them extremely significant. Mr. Speaker, I think we should realize that in a village, things do not work exactly the way they do in our big cities. It often happens that the grocer or the owner of the general store gives customers credit.
There may be only one grocer in the whole village. So imagine the following scenario: Mr. or Mrs. so-and-so is expecting a very important letter and, before these changes, would have gone to the post office, and since confidentiality is the rule, there are no problems. But because of Canada Post's decision, Mrs. so-and-so now has to go to the grocer where she has run up a bill of $200 or $300 or $400, and it has now been two, three, four or five months since she was able to meet her financial obligations. Mrs. so-and-so is more or less being told she has no choice and that she has to go to this particular location to pick up her mail.
I heard another comment which I also thought was very apt. People feel, and rightly so, that mail should be a confidential and private matter. You must understand that at a convenience store or grocery, for any Tom, Dick or Harry, it is the clerk who is there when the customer arrives who must deliver or receive material that for many people is extremely confidential.
There is also something else. You must understand that in these villages, for the past few years, in most cases this coincides with the coming to power of this Government. These small post offices have been tied to schedules that are, for all practical purposes, unreasonable and poorly thought out. It is not at all unusual, for example, to go to a country post office at
12.30	or 1 p.m. to find it closed. It is not at all unusual to go at
8.30	or 8.45 a.m. and still find it closed. Indeed, hundreds, even thousands, of people who would be entitled to get their mail find the door closed. What do they do? They leave, they go to the next town, to a larger centre, to buy their stamps, to do in a way what could and should be done in the village. So at the end of the year, the financial results of rural post offices are not as good as urban post offices'. This is used as a pretext to say that it just does not pay. Let us get rid of it, it does not pay! Now, I think it is just the opposite of what we should do: keep the post offices in these regions and in the countryside, provide more services, give more opportunity to those who are used to the services to have them and thus make these operations much more profitable.
Mr. Speaker, my constituency is quite rural and I have many times seen how important the mail is.
To observe this basic importance of the mail service, several times in the morning I have followed the rural mailman who uses his vehicle to distribute mail from house to house on country roads and in the countryside. To my great surprise, I noticed that not only is he waited for, but in very many cases people are at their box waiting for their mail. In cases where people are not there before the mail arrives, in the next few seconds or minutes, they come to claim it. I think that for many people, it is the only means of communication, a very
May 12, 1988

important one in every respect. You must also understand that for most of the people who live in these regions, this is how they get their pay cheques, information and printed matter. And the services which all these Canadians receive are basic and essential services, so much so that the mere suggestion that they might be reduced or cut has a tragic impact.
Mr. Speaker, again last week I got a letter from the municipal corporation of the parish of Saint-Remi-de-Tingwick, as follows: "Following the March 7 regular sitting, the municipality of Saint-Remi-de-Tingwick urges the residents to sign a petition against closing the post office and reducing our normal postal services. " Sir, with this letter I enclose the petition signed by the residents of Saint-Remi to voice their strong opposition to closing the post office and reducing normal postal services.
Mr. Speaker, I know that community and practically everybody in the village signed the petition. In light of the famous report which was unanimously endorsed, it seems to me the human, decent and normally acceptable approach would have been to consult the people, give them an explanation, and ask them what they think their post office should be like. I can tell you that out in the country the post office is very often a meeting place, and more often than not the only federal Government presence. As I see it, it would not be unrealistic or unreasonable to suggest that these post offices can be maintained and, as far as I am concerned, turned into profitable operations.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I take a hint from my colleague for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) who not only criticizes agressively the Government's attitude on that matter but also comes up with explanations or proposals for the Corporation to get extra revenues in order to provide a decent service that would be acceptable to all. At one point the Hon. Member suggested selling space on the trucks. Mr. Speaker, we have seen a multitude of new companies go into business in the last few years. Whether it is Purolator, Selco, or this or that, to my knowledge those companies are not losing any money. So the Corporation is depriving itself of substantial revenues that could be used to provide decent, acceptable service in rural areas. We have the example of telephone service. The cost is the same for both urban and rural areas, and this brings in enough income for everyone in Canada to enjoy reasonable, fair and equitable telephone rates. Through intensified use of those new services, the Corporation could therefore get the income needed to balance its books.
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude by suggesting that there is tremendous discontent, and this week's latest survey explains part of the story at Canada Post.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity today to participate on this opposition day motion put forward by my Party concerning
Supply
what the Government has done to Canada's postal service. I know from my records that I have participated twice before in opposition day debates on this subject, which is an indication of the importance of postal service to residents of the approximately 120 communities in my riding of Kenora-Rainy River.
I am very glad to say that our spokesman on postal issues, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper), although not able to speak to this particular motion, has consistently and in a very committed and dedicated fashion addressed the concerns of both rural and urban dwellers in regard to Canada Post service. I must say that this is a question in which vigilance has indeed been the price of continued service for many across the country.
The Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann) in his speech seemed very taken with the first part of the motion, that is, that the Government had instructed Canada Post to cut back on postal services to Canadians living in rural areas. He seemed to feel that the Government was innocent of that particular charge. However, that innocence is something that I believe on examination of the facts is quite impossible to maintain. In fact, the Government has ordered those cuts just as effectively, if not as specifically, as if it had gone to regional managers and individual postmasters and said: "Cut this service. Cut that rural route. Cut out that particular box".
What we are seeing in the case of Canada Post is management by financial control. For some years Canada Post had been running a deficit, and the Government simply said: "Well, you are not going to be able to run a deficit any more. We are cutting you off. You can deliver what postal service you can. You can raise revenues or cut the costs, but you are not going to get the money from the federal exchequer". That, of course, is management by financial control.
Anyone who has studied business in any depth whatsoever knows that when there is a deficit there are three ways that the deficit can be covered. The first is by borrowing, something which the Government ruled out. It ruled it out in a fashion which very adversely affected the potential that Canada Post had a few years ago to decrease its deficit, and perhaps even to make a profit, and also to deliver service to Canadians. But the Government ruled out the possibility of the corporation borrowing for the purchases of new equipment for the purpose of parcel handling which would have enabled it to compete with the couriers in the inter-city markets in particular where courier companies are doing so well because of the Government's obstruction of Canada Post's potential entry into the market. It also ruled out the purchase of other sorting equipment and mail processing equipment.
The other two ways of eliminating a deficit are to raise revenues and to cut costs. I must say that I feel that Canada Post has not been effective enough in terms of raising revenues, in terms of collecting more for some of its under-priced services and in terms of extending some of those services which

May 12, 1988
Supply
have good revenue potential. Instead it seems to have concentrated on cutting back on its costs, particularly as regards the rural and suburban service networks, but which also affects urban offices as well in some of our major centres.
Because the Government has framed its instructions in dollar terms rather than in specific orders cannot absolve the Government of responsibility for the effects. Simply translating instructions into dollars cannot take away the fact that it is the Government that is behind these costs. Canada Post is being treated essentially as order takers and told to get on with the job, which is to balance the budget. Thus we have the consequences that my constituents have felt and which constituents in rural ridings across the country have felt and seen. In many cases they have very drastically affected the whole way in which they see their community.
We have had cases where the only building in a community that flew the Canadian flag no longer flies it because the Post Office has been closed, or it has been privatized to a hard-pressed local retail outlet which has been under all sorts of financial and psychological pressure to take on the service, a service which is very poorly paid for by Canada Post. The Crown corporation seems to expect, essentially, that grocery store to provide a service on a grace and favour sort of basis at rates which in fact if they were salary rates would not be allowable under any provincial labour law in the country. However, it expects these people to do it because it knows that it has them over a barrel once the post office is gone.

Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege to represent my Party in February 1988 at the founding conference of the Vision of Rural Dignity organization.
Mr. Speaker, I travelled to a village with a population of 600 on the South Shore in Quebec of the St. Lawrence river, to attend that conference along with more than 800 people who came from all across rural Quebec, in addition to people from the area itself, and also from other provinces, including Newfoundland, Saskatchewan, New Brunswick and Ontario. They gathered to establish an organization that will speak for rural communities faced with postal service shutdowns.
Mr. Speaker, Visions of Rural Dignity has experienced significant growth, even since that founding conference was held.
This organization now speaks for all communities in this country who are threatened by postal service cancellation and post office shut downs.
But despite these efforts, and I must congratulate those who have set up this rural organization for their dedication and commitment, rural Canada has lost 194 post offices in the last couple of years through closing-down or privatization and, at the end of the month, this figure will have reached the 200 mark.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that Canada Post will not stop after closing-down these 200 post offices because their internal
budget forecasts a profit, a surplus of some 38 million dollars in the next fiscal year for Dignite rurale du Canada and its work.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that, in such a situation, Canada Post should be studying ways of improving postal services to rural Canadians rather than reducing them further, as we see in this budget.
Mr. Speaker, Dignite rurale du Canada has become the main spokesman against cuts in rural postal services . . .

There have also been organizations which have been formed to fight against the use of these pernicious supermailboxes.
I am afraid to say that there has been a great deal of blatant propaganda put out by Canada Post about these so-called supermailboxes. The very name should have alerted us to the wool being pulled over our eyes. Of course there have been public opinion surveys very cleverly phrased and presented about the supermailboxes. The message through these surveys has always been: "How do you see a supermailbox compared to door-to-door delivery?'' They have not been: "How do you see a supermailbox compared to a green mailbox or compared to no delivery at all?"
Supermailboxes for all their presentation and the attractive PR that was put out when they were introduced have encountered some problems. We recall the almost commando descent by Canada Post technicians on, I believe it was, St. John's, Newfoundland, in order to fix up some of the problems with supermailboxes that were giving out mail to the wrong people. There were mechanical failures. They have become an eyesore. Recently, the Ontario Municipal Board even reduced the taxes of some people who had supermailboxes put in front of their homes.
The installation of these supermailboxes was not properly planned, either in terms of their siting or in terms of the maintenance of the site. In many cases, they presented an obstruction for snowplows. Another complaint was that they were often placed in areas which proved unsafe for those making use of them. With the advent of the supermailbox, we had a gratuitous and unnecessary mixing of pedestrian and vehicle traffic-something that obviously ought to have been foreseen as a hazard. Generally, they were looked upon as an eyesore and an inconvenience, something that people would only put up with if offered no alternative. It is the fact that no alternative has been offered that has led to some of the anomalous situations which we now face. Not only are the supermailboxes seen as inefficient and ineffective, but fundamentally unfair for those forced to use them.
We have a situation in the community of Fort Frances where of the four homes at one intersection, three receive door-to-door delivery, with one being forced to use a supermailbox,
May 12, 1988

that house having been built after the extension of door-to-door delivery had been abolished by Canada Post. That is a very strange situation. It gives one the feeling that one's neighbours are being somehow regarded as superior, and certainly they are inasmuch as they are being offered a superior service.
Paragraph (c) of the motion makes the point that hundreds of thousands of Canadians have been made second-class citizens when it comes to the provision of postal service. That is a telling accusation, and I believe it to be one that is eminently sustainable. It is one that applies not just to the consumers of the postal service, but to those involved in providing the postal service itself.
In my own community, I am aware of a tourist operator who now faces a 65-kilometre round trip to pick up his mail, whereas previously service was provided via a rural route. In order to save costs for Canada Post, individual members of the public are being put to additional cost and inconvenience in order to get their mail.
If this type of measure were to be properly evaluated, I think it would be seen as a false economy. While Canada Post Corporation is saving money, it is doing so on the backs of those it is supposed to be serving.
There are reserve communities of the Nishnawbe Aski Nation in my constituency which can only be reached by air, and for such communities there are numerous inequities in respect of the postal service provided. Mr. Eno Anderson, the chairman of the Shibogama Tribal Council has been following the matter up with me on a regular basis. He has raised with me the fact that the clerks who carry out the postal duty are underpaid for the time that they put in; that often they turn up at the airport only to find out that there is no mail on board.
In those instances, they receive no compensation. Nor are they compensated for taking the mail from the airport to the post office, which might be up to 15 kilometres. As well, they are forced to work on a sporadic and intermittent basis, going from periods of very high activity, very high pressure, to having to take care of the details of the job, when really they should be having free time.
There is also the matter of the irregularity of mail delivery, and the fact that many communities only receive mail once a week. There have been also been problems for contractors. I am aware of one contractor who held a route for many years, providing excellent service year-in and year-out, who was replaced by an individual who put in a lower bid, only to find, within one week, that he could not deliver the service for the amount of the bid.
Canada Post eventually went back to the same contractor. But, at what cost? It went back to the person who knew how to do the job, the person who had done it for years. But, at what cost in terms of disruption, in terms of stress and strain, both for the original contractor and the individual who had
Supply
submitted the low bid? That individual had obviously been sucked into submitting a bid that he could not live with.
I am aware of one contractor with over 35 years of service in different capacities with Canada Post who is now getting out of the business. He knows that the next time his route is up for bid, others tempted by the possibility of acquiring the contract will bid unrealistically low, only to find themselves handicapped in trying to deliver the appropriate level of service.
We have had mailbox shortages in our communities. Those losing rural route service come into town to acquire a mailbox only to find that there are none available. While there is a waiting list for mailboxes, rural routes are being cut.
There are many cases where, if provincial labour laws were to apply, Canada Post would be taken to court. For example, Mr. Speaker, I quote from Dignite Rurale du Canada:

"The statistics for this province show that under these contracts, the Postmaster gets only one-fifth of his present salary, which works out to $2,000-52,400 per year, or between 47 cents and 83 cents an hour".

I also have an article from The Toronto Star, an article which speaks of some of the problems facing family-run convenience stores, the so-called Mom and Pop convenience stores, in trying to oblige Canada Post in setting up postal outlets, in some cases under something of a subtle threat that if they do not, they will be penalized. But, in trying to oblige Canada Post, they have ended up being paid ridiculously small sums of money for the services they are providing.
In the few minutes remaining, I should like to consolidate the case that fair and equitable and equal postal service across Canada is not simply a justice issue or matter of equity, or a matter of how we view ourselves as Canadians, as equals, but a matter of economic efficiency-and this is something that should appeal to my friends opposite.
To review the history very briefly, the first penny post was introduced in England under the leadership of Roland Hill, in 1840. It cost one penny to send a piece of mail to any part of the kingdom. Before that, mail moved by the 19th century equivalent of today's couriers, the stage coach, with those using the service paying a sixpence or a shilling to have a letter taken 100 miles.
With the introduction of the penny post, mail could be sent anywhere in the kingdom for one penny. Well, I need hardly make the contrast between a public service that functions on a utility basis and a privatized service that was run simply for profit.
Perhaps that might have some of my friends opposite in fact cheering for the profit opportunities inherent in a private service; but let us not forget the very nature of our federal country, the very nature of the remoteness of some communities, the vast distances between communities-all of which, of

May 12, 1988
Supply
course, render all of the comparisons that the Government Members have been making to the U.S. postal service irrelevant. Let us not forget that we should see Canadians as Canadians, wherever they live. I am very glad to see the Hon. Member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Suluk), here today. I believe that he could talk very eloquently of the problems of remote communities.
Let us remember that there were two reasons for the establishment of a federal Government in the first place in Canada. One was national defence; the second was to ensure that the mail was run effectively. Let us not forget that the Canadian flag flying over post offices is a very visible reminder, and in some communities the only reminder, of the fact that we have a federal Government in Canada, a Government whose duty it is to bind all Canadians together.
When the Government fails to make provision for Canada Post to perform that essential equity function, it undercuts the whole significance of Canadian unity. The solution is not for the Government to subsidize Canada Post indefinitely, or without a bottom to the funds that are made available; the solution is for the Government to allow Canada Post to compete effectively. The solution is for the Government to give Canada Post realistic and reasonable subsidies to carry out that very important national unity function that Canada Post has served heretofore, a function which is so endangered by the imposition of purely financial goals and financial measures on this most essential of all Crown corporations.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz), on a question or comment.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciated hearing the speech given by the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry), a Member for whom I have a great deal of respect. He certainly debates issues with eloquence and fairness. He did not use a lot of rhetoric as some Members across the way have done today.
Having said that, I want to read part of the opposition motion:
That this House condemn the government for its total and absolute failure
to provide fair and equitable postal service to all Canadians by:
(b) installing "supermailboxes"-
I want to make a couple of points and then pose a question. Where I live in the Town of Fort Erie, which is a community of about 25,000 people, there is no mail delivery. There have been what we call group boxes for a number of years, as long as I can remember, which I suppose today if they were installed somewhere could be called supermailboxes. People have used those and, to the best of my knowledge, they have used them without complaint. I drive a mile to the post office to get my mail. We have never had delivery in my part of the town. The place where I live, Ridgeway, which is part of Fort Erie, may have a population of about 2,000 people. We have always gone to the post office and picked up our mail.
Let us look at two other areas in the Town of Fort Erie, the old part, where the population might consist of about 12,000 people, and Crescent Park in the Town of Fort Erie which has a population of perhaps 3,000 people. Those people have mail delivery, which leaves us with a population of about 10,000 people in the Town of Fort Erie who do not receive mail delivery. Yet the New Democrats are condemning the Government for its failure to provide fair and equitable postal service to all Canadians.
Is the Hon. Member implying that those 10,000 Canadians, including myself, should have mail delivery service? Is he implying that everyone in the town should have it, that just because 15,000 people have mail delivery the other 10,000 should, otherwise it is unfair and inequitable?
I want to remind the Hon. Member that I pay-I am not sure because my wife usually writes the cheque-about $12 a year for a postal box. We get the biggest one we can.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext: Just $12?

It may be $15, I do not know. We pay for the privilege of getting in the car or walking, if we feel well enough, to go to the post office to pick up the mail, whereas other people who pay the same rate of postage, 37 cents have their mail delivered to their homes. If the Member wants to look at that and say that is inequitable, that is his privilege. Is that what the Hon. Member is saying?
I have two questions. The first is with regard to the boxes which I have indicated are group mailboxes which help those people in the part of the town in which I live, and the second concerns the inequity of those 10,000 people in my town who have never had mail delivery. I have lived there 61 years and never once have I had mail delivery.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Fort Erie (Mr. Fretz), for his question and say that Fort Erie must be a marvellous place to live if he has spent 61 years there. In my opinion, he really does not show the wear and tear of those 61 years.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext: Because he walks to the post office instead of sitting at home.
Hear, hear!

Perhaps it is his daily walk to the Post Office, Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary said.
I would have to say that the Hon. Member must recognize that he places me at a disadvantage in discussion of his particular circumstance. He surely cannot believe that in my 18 years of residence in Canada, none of which has ever been within 100 miles of Fort Erie, that I could have attained as intimate a knowledge of the geography of that community as he has in his 61 years.
To address the question directly, in terms of equity of postal service, there should be measures, and my understanding is
May 12, 1988

there are measures in some context but not in others, by which growing areas qualify for door-to-door delivery. Density must play a part. I learned from my experience in planning legislation in Ontario that there are many cases where development occurs in a patchwork fashion. It occurs in strips or in isolated mini-subdivisions where I do not think people are looking for home delivery of mail by virtue of the rural nature, shall we say, of the surroundings in which they have decided to live. If Canada Post had sets of rules that covered these sorts of situations which were applied equally across the country, then that would constitute an equitable mail service. I am not suggesting that all group mailboxes, the old style green mailboxes, should not be replaced with supermailboxes. I think that supermailboxes are a useful tool for the type of situation that presumably once existed in the area in which the Hon. Member lives but which now, as a result of the growth of the communities, I am sure under progressive leadership, no longer pertains.
Are you crossing the floor or what?
Oh, oh!

Equity does not consist in the provision of identical service. It consists of addressing the concerns of those people who feel deprived or disadvantaged by a particular type of service. Perhaps the Hon. Member is suggesting, without wanting to state it openly, that people who receive door-to-door delivery should pay an annual fee similar to the fee that the Hon. Member and I pay. I do not have a big mailbox like the Hon. Member for Erie. All my mail comes here. I would rather see the fees waived in the case of the mailboxes in the small post offices, but we know that might lead to a proliferation of requests for the boxes. The door-to-door fee might be an easy way of resolving Canada Post's deficit, but I do not think it would be universally popular. While I feel that the provision of mailboxes is a Canada Post responsibility, we have to recognize that there will always be market factors ruling in that sort of case.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of State and Minister of State (Treasury Board)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
speechtext:
Not to worry, Mr. Speaker. I am pleased to have this opportunity to enter today's debate on this motion. The Hon. Minister responsible for Canada Post is in his riding today and I am happy to participate and put forward the Government's point of view with respect to this motion. I think I should point out a few things before getting into some
Supply
personal observations which I am able to make on behalf of the Minister and on behalf of myself with respect to the improved service of Canada Post.
First, Canada Post is a very large corporate employer in Canada. It employs approximately 47,000 people. It is a corporation which was set up under the previous Government to try to bring into place some new management methods, and to improve postal service for Canadians. In doing so it has made some very fundamental corporate changes. The focus of the entire corporate plan is on service. The whole purpose of its existence is to provide Canadians with efficient, reliable and affordable postal service.
The five-year corporate plan which was presented today is also a business plan. We do not see any conflict between providing a service and the objectives of a well run business. I think it is obvious that if a business does not provide good service to its customers, it will not stay in business, whether it is providing a product like automobiles or postal service.
The key elements of Canada Post's service thrust are reliability, accessibility, delivery and value for money. First I want to deal with the question of reliability.
Canada Post has taken several steps to ensure that operations are properly monitored by control centres and that they are managed according to corporate systems seven days a week and for 24 hours each day. We have instituted a policy of auditing, through independent auditors, the performance of the delivery standards. Clarkson Gordon has been retained by Canada Post to do this job, and it recently released its findings.
I point out to the House that Canada Post is the only postal service in the world that has its performance standards publicly measured by an independent auditing firm. The second quarterly report was released last month. It has shown a continued and steady improvement in service performance and Canada Post is working to improve that performance even more by identifying any problems it has in the system and by correcting them.
Another aspect of this improvement in service is to improve access. This means making it easier for Canadians to buy the products and services and to pick up parcels and mail requiring a signature. I point out that the corporation is doing this in a big way. Canada Post already has more retail outlets than all the banks and financial institutions in Canada combined. Over the next several years, the number of locations where Canadians can go to purchase postal products and services will increase even further from 13,800 to 18,000.
On a personal note, I want to point out that two or three years ago when the present Minister was made responsible for Canada Post, I said to him one day at 10 minutes after six: "Harvie, here is a package of cigarettes and a stamp. Where do you buy the cigarettes? You can buy those anywhere. Where do you buy the stamp?"

May 12, 1988
Supply
Obviously, to buy a stamp, one has to find a post office that will sell a stamp. That is the point. Why should Canadians be restricted when buying stamps when they can buy lottery tickets and cigarettes anywhere 24 hours a day? That is the point of the improved access we are driving at.
The Opposition would have all postage stamps in Canada sold from nine 'til five, five days a week, in post offices. Our attitude is, let us make it easy to mail things. Let us not restrict it to certain places the way the Opposition wants us to do. Let us make it easy for Canadians to buy postage stamps. Why not? Why should it be such a sacred thing to sell a postage stamp? That is the whole idea behind the privatization of the post office facilities.
I cannot for the life of me figure out why the NDP and the Liberals do not want Canadians to have that kind of accessibility. Why not? Why not let Canadians buy postage stamps anywhere, just like cigarettes and candy? What is the big secret about it? I want to know that. I want to hear from opposition Members about that.
That is what we are doing about accessibility, and we are doing it through business, through that partnership which can exist with the private sector. We are expanding facilities. I want to explain this to my friends because they have blinders on. I want to tell them what is happening in my riding in the Township of Oro, a rural township, and my friend, the Elon. Member for Elumboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), will know about this.
Previously, there were three sub-post offices in the Township of Oro. What were their hours? Their hours were from 8.15 to 12.30, an hour off for lunch, and closed at 5.15. That was for only five days a week. On Saturday, it was 8 'til 12, no service Saturday afternoon, Saturday evening or Sunday. That was the situation in Shanty Bay, Oro Station and Hawkestone.
Now we are privatizing. My constituents in Oro Township will be able to get stamps in three places, the same villages, Shanty Bay, Oro Station and Hawkestone. Guess what? These are the new hours of operation: 7 a.m. until 10 p.m. in the first location at Shanty Bay. It is a little restricted in Oro Station. It is only open from eight in the morning until nine at night, and the same in Hawkestone. Guess what? All three of them are open Sundays. Isn't that terrible? Now my constituents in Oro Township can buy stamps on Sundays. My friends in the Opposition, the NDP and the Liberals, do not like buying stamps on Sundays.
That is the kind of increased access to service we are giving. Not only that, but at Fuda's Marketplace on Highway 11, they are putting in a new operation. My constituents will get three locations with expanded hours and a new fourth location. That is what Canada Post is doing. However, the Opposition is not bragging about that, it says that we are restricting service.
We are expanding the delivery network. We notice that our friends are pressing for expanded door-to-door delivery. Let me talk about door-to-door delivery.

We are struggling to bring the NDP into the 1990s and new methods of doing things. It is just unfortunate that they cannot get up to speed.
We are looking at value for money. When we brought in the corporate plan last year, we announced that we were going to continue to adjust our basic letter rates annually to compensate for the impact of inflation and other expenditure increases. The planned rate increases in the basic letter rate during the next five years will continue to be below the rate of inflation as projected by economic indicators. Canada Post announced today that it is gazetting a proposal for a rate increase to take place January 1, 1989. The increase in the basic postal rate will be one cent. That is 2.5 per cent for a standard letter. There will be other products affected by the rate increase and that is available in the information package that was distributed.
Even with this modest rate increase, Canadians will be paying the second lowest postage rate in the world when you compare average wages. In fact, using the same measurement, they pay roughly the same today as they did 32 years ago.
The NDP say they want door-to-door delivery, and all we have to do is raise the price of a stamp to 60 cents. I cannot understand why the NDP wants to raise the price of stamps to 60 cents. Why not adopt some modern methods and put in the supermailboxes, do what we can to improve things, but not give door-to-door delivery to everyone as the NDP suggests and raise the price of stamps to 60 cents? That ignores market realities.
We are monitoring the price tolerances of our products because we realize that Canada Post is in a highly competitive market. About 80 per cent of its volume is generated by business. If we exceed that price tolerance then business will look elsewhere to have its products delivered. Therefore, when we look at rate increases, we are really reflecting the reality of the market-place. To do that we have to increase our volume so that we can be competitive. We are restructuring our products and services to better reflect the requirements of the market-place and improving our courier service in the face of very keen competition. We are doing this so that we can get Canada Post back to the place it once enjoyed in this market.
This fiscal year is very significant for Canada Post because this is the year that the ink goes from red to black. After losing under the Liberals several million dollars a year, the Post Office is now going to break even under the Conservatives. For the first time in 25 years it is forecasting a modest profit from operations.
Canada Post is trying to build a postal service for the future, not for the horse and buggy age of the NDP. To do that it has to finance new equipment and introduce needed innovations to provide a truly modern, reliable and efficient service. says that it is not enough to point the figure at Canada Post but at the Government, given the fact that Canada Post is only carrying out the wishes of a Government that takes the position that the deficit has to be eliminated within two years. Further, it is the position of this Government that the Post Office, in eliminating its deficit within two years, cannot investigate revenue generating areas which would put it into competition with the private sector, including such endeavours as direct mail, the provision of telex services, and so forth.
The postal corporation has had its hands tied. On the one hand, it has been given a mandate by the Government to-

... make up the deficit, but at the same time, it does have the necessary tools to do so, because it is not allowed for example to do direct mailing or to undertake other income generating projects.
I shoud like to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that it is not the management of Canada Post but the union which launched a project in Calgary some time ago in an attempt to find some ways or means to generate more incomes for Canada Post. Finally, it is management and the Government who refuse to approve services which could compete with the private sector.
It is rather funny, Mr. Speaker, that the private sector can compete with Canada Post but that Canada Post may not compete with the private sector.
I think that it is a matter of bad management by the Government and that it will have to pay dearly on the mail issue during the next election.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Questions and comments. The Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Brightwell).
[ English ]

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) has demonstrated, once again, her great ability for overstatement. Perhaps it is because, as she has said, she gets her information from clerks in variety stores. Maybe this is an example of how the Liberals get all of their information and how unsubstantiated it is.
Oh, shame! And what is wrong with clerks in variety stores? Shame! Are you an elitist?

The Hon. Member did in fact say that she got her information from a clerk in a variety store. She then came out with a crushing proposition, that being that governments should intrude on private industry, that governments should compete with private industry.
I would be interested in hearing what private industry would have to say about the proposition that Government should go out and try to take away business from those earning a living from it.

Go back under your shell.
May 12, 1988

I take exception to the Hon. Member's assertion that it is unfair for those who do not have home delivery. I represent a riding in which more than 50 per cent of my constituents have never had home delivery of mail. On many farms, the mailbox can be a distance of well over 600 feet from the house. For other services, one has to travel to the post office in the nearest village or town. Yet, the Hon. Member wants everybody to have home delivery. That is just simply not possible.
What does the Hon. Member have to say in respect of the handicapped who live in areas that do not have door-to-door mail service? How do those people get their mail? Why are the handicapped living in our cities to be treated differently from those who live in the rural areas?

Mr. Speaker, I think what we have heard are two ridiculous comments rolled into one. First of all, what is wrong with getting information from a store clerk? Perhaps the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Brightwell) got elected by talking only to lawyers and doctors, and bank presidents, but where I come from it is important that parliamentarians speak for all of the people. An individual working in a store has as much right to voice an opinion
A clerk in a variety store can provide you with postal information?

Mr. Speaker, in point of fact I was reading a letter from a professor. Perhaps the Hon. Member will accept the information since it comes from a professor. What the Hon. Member is saying is that it is fine if the information comes from a professor, but not if it comes from a store clerk. There is no question that in rural Canada the handicapped find it difficult to get to a post office, to get to their mailbox.
And you do not feel sorry for them?

What the Hon. Member seems to be saying is that we ought to inflict the same situation on the handicapped living in new developments. If you recognize that there is something wrong with a system that does not provide adequate access for the disabled, surely you would not want to add to that.
If in fact the Hon. Member for Perth is truly interested in integrating the disabled into the mainstream of the community, surely he will recognize that we ought to do all that we can in new developments to accommodate the disabled. In addition to architecturally designing new communities in a fashion that will permit the disabled to live independently within the community, we should also provide them with accessible mail service-and supermailboxes are simply not accessible for the disabled. We are supposed to be moving, in 1988, toward more accessibility for the disabled, not less.
Granting the Hon. member's proposition that it is extremely difficult for handicapped persons in rural areas to get to a post office, surely that is something that we should not add to elsewhere.
Supply
You do not care about the handicapped in the rural areas?

I am not saying that at all. You are suggesting that because there is a difficult situation that exists in the rural areas of this country, we should exacerbate that situation in the future by eliminating door-to-door mail service. If you view the lack of accessibility to mail service to be a problem for the handicapped in rural Canada, surely you should be speaking in support of extending that service, which is the aim of this debate today.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), on a question or comment, to be followed by the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Fraleigh).

Mr. Speaker, we have a situation in my constituency which sounds to be remarkably similar to what has gone on in the Westdale area of the Hon. Member's constituency of Hamilton East.
In the Glebe area of Ottawa, an area within a 10 or 15 minute walk of the House of Commons, we had a similar situation, where one day, without prior announcement, the Post Office decided to move the registered mail and parcel pick-up services from the Fourth Avenue Post Office branch, a branch which has been at the heart of that community for a number of years, to a commercial establishment on Main Street, and when it did not work out at that location, it was moved to a grocery store at the corner of Fifth Avenue and Bank, and then to premises in the upper level of the Fifth Avenue Court complex, and from there to a confectionery on O'Connor Street, with the result that it is now removed from the area where people shop. While it has been there for some time now, goodness knows where it will end up.
The Glebe Community Association tried to arrange for a meeting with the Minister responsible for Canada Post, but were unsuccessful.
Why should a community association be denied the right to meet with the responsible Minister?
I met with people from the Glebe community, and together we talked to officials from the Rideau Division of Canada Post. They went away saying that they would get back to us, and in fact they did, saying that they were not prepared to make any changes. We were told that because other people had accepted this deterioration of service, we, too, should be happy, and that, no, we could not talk to the Minister. They took the position that because the Post Office is a Crown corporation, they were not going to listen to us.
What kind of redress is that?
. .. Mr. Speaker in the Ottawa area, the National Capital region which should be bilingual, it is increasingly inpossible

May 12, 1988
Supply
for those who wish to be served in French to obtain such services in post offices due to privatization. Is this warranted when the Canada Post Corporation is a national service, a federal service?

I would like the Hon. Member to comment on those problems which seem to be found not only in her constituency but in Ottawa Centre and everywhere else.

Mr. Speaker, I dare say that it is not only a problem in Ottawa Centre. The problem I raised with respect to Westdale was actually in the riding of Hamilton West, which is held by a Conservative colleague. He has been the recipient of a letter also, although I do not know what he has done about it. I understand as well the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-d'Anjou is facing a similar situation in his own area. This is why I made the point, and I am sorry the Hon. Member who spoke earlier did not understand, that the Post Office is still taking the position with respect to the Westdale facility that it is not closing, that it is a mere cutback in service.
Because the Government saw the big uprising, the revolt and the kind of political haemorrhaging it suffered on the issue of the rural post offices, even in the urban areas it is intending to kill by amputation-it is not a complete strangulation-first it will amputate the hand, then the arm, and then the rest of the body. Eventually the Westdale Post Office will probably close.
The Government, because it realized that it had such a political backlash when it closed the rural post offices, again has a secret agenda. The secret agenda probably will not become fully apparent for another couple of years. How can one say that the Westdale Post Office will remain fully operational when one of the essential services is being farmed off to the private sector? Obviously if the intention was to keep the service at optimum level, you would not see part of the service being taken, split off and given to a pharmacy, a confectionery or whatever.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to direct some comments in support of the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Brightwell) with regard to those millions of Canadians who for 100 years, since the start of postal service, have walked to pick up their mail. When they got to the end of their walk, they also paid for the privilege of having a box in which the Post Office put the mail. Those people are not complaining in any particular way. It is the way they have lived for 100 years and they do not expect any change.
I want to point out that we do have inclement weather in small-town Canada. The Hon. Member may not have been out there lately. We have seniors, we have handicapped people, the same as the Hon. Member has in her riding in small-town Canada. Does the Hon. Member know how people get their mail? Their neighbours get it for them. Isn't it an awful saying that a neighbour would have to help someone who is handicapped or who is a senior? The Hon. Member can shake her
head if she likes, but it is the way we live in Canada, maybe not in the never-never world in which the Hon. Member lives.
1 can understand how people who have had the privilege of having their mail dropped through a slot in their front door would hate to give that up. But I ask the Member to think about those people who for 100 years have paid for the privilege of having to walk to a post office. The Hon. Member can sit down because I am not finished yet.
This is supposed to be a question.
Ask a question.
The Hon. Member should be careful or he will have another heart attack.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: This is a chance for questions and comments. If there is a question which the Hon. Member would like to put, he still has an opportunity to do so. Does the Hon. Member have a question?
No, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I do not understand whether I was in the same room as the Hon. Member or whether it was something I said that went in one ear and out the other. I never in any way disparaged or said that people who live in rural Canada in some way are or should be treated as second-class citizens. On the contrary, what 1 said to the Hon. Member for Perth was that if there is a problem in the delivery of the service then surely it is our job as Members to make it better and not bring it to the lowest common denominator of service.
The Member's suggestion is a wonderful one that neighbours will go and get one's mail. I do not know what inner city community the Member has been to lately but in my community I have a section of apartment dwellers. If you look at the average rate at which people move, it is usually once every three years.
In Strawberry Hills they are not getting delivery. They get supermailboxes.
Is it inner city?

I live in a densely populated community. I will take the Hon. Member there and show it to him. If we could live in a society where we could count on our friends and neighbours, that would be terrific. I think it would be wonderful to have such a close-knit way of life. Unfortunately, that is not the reality in 1988 in most major urban areas. There are many people who live in communities who do not know the names of their next door neighbours. I am not saying that is right or it is a situation which should be imitated, but it is reality. The Hon. Member suggests that with supermailboxes people will be able to call on friends and neighbours, but that is not always possible. Would that it were so, I think we have something which he should cherish and defend. The Hon. Member has to recognize that in planning Canada Post must
May 12, 1988

look at reality and not the ideal world that in most urban centres does not exist.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate. The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez).

Mr. Speaker, I want to say that the House owes a debt to the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) in presenting this motion for consideration today. I want to put the motion once again on the record:
That this House condemn the government for its total and absolute failure
to provide fair and equitable postal service to all Canadians-
I heard the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) speak about the great defence of postal workers who were out on strike and that the Liberal Party was all together on the issue. It is about the only issue the Liberals have been all together on in recent years. I am sure CUPW and the posties would be delighted to know that they brought the Liberal caucus together. There is a uniting force here.
Oh, oh!

Who does the Hon. Member think she is kidding, Mr. Speaker? Was I on another planet when the Liberals were in Government and Bryce Mackasey accused the postal workers of being Marxist, that they were destroying the Post Office? Did not this whole process of bad human relations within the Post Office not get exacerbated by Liberal Governments? I recall Bryce Mackasey saying: "I know the problem with the Post Office. I know what it is. It is Marxism. They are all Marxists". His brilliant deduction was that the problem with the Post Office was Marxism. We do not have Mr. Mackasey with us any more. We now have a Conservative Government.
We didn't talk about replacement workers.

No, the Hon. Member did not talk about replacement workers. But what the Liberals were looking for was a scapegoat on which to hang the problems of the Post Office instead of doing what any sensible Minister in Government ought to do. Any Minister should take a look at the Post Office and see how to improve the service and should not look for scapegoats on which to blame problems. That is where it all started. What if one were to extend this logic of the Government with respect to the postal services in this country to other essential services, for example, the fire department? Can you imagine the fire department running on a profit basis? Imagine charging people so that the fire department could generate a profit. That reminds me of the year 13 B.C. when Marcus Crassus owned the only fire department in Rome, and when there was a fire, they would call Marcus Crassus out and he would arrive at the scene of the fire and start negotiating with the home owner the cost of putting out the fire. History clearly shows that Marcus Crassus, in this way, became one of the wealthiest land owners in Rome.
Supply
Imagine if we were to extend this logic of the god of profit that the Conservative Government worships, the logic which says that the Post Office has to make a profit. How crazy it would be to extend that to the fire department. The Government would be laughed out of this place if it did that.
What about the police force? Do we expect the police departments across Canada to show profits? No, we do not. We recognize that fire protection and police protection are services to which all Canadians are entitled, and we do not provide first class and second class service. The same is true of garbage collection.
I am not aware of the fact that there are two kinds of garbage collection services. They do not go to Forest Hills in Toronto to pick up the garbage with white gloves. I understand they used to go around to the back door, but they have cut that out now. The fact is that the same service is provided, whether it is once a week or twice a week.
The same should be true of the Post Office. In fact, I would suggest that the Post Office is probably the only visible indication of the federal Government in every little community across Canada. It seems to me that in most small towns, there is a post office which flies the Canadian flag. It is the national presence in those towns. It is a unifying element.
In the small town that I lived in in northern Ontario for some 10 glorious years, the Town of Coniston, the post office was right in the centre of town. After the mail had been delivered and sorted, everyone would go to the post office. It became the social centre. The retired folk would meet there. They would see each other and chat there.
What has happened now? The Minister, speaking earlier in this debate, said that when the Conservatives came into office, there was a $300 million deficit in the post office. It seems that the Government did not bat an eyelash when it had to fork over $1 billion to bail out a bank. It did not make much fuss about that. However, to provide quality mail service across Canada, it does not want to spend that $300 million.
The Post Office had some options and the Government had some options. The Government wanted to show a profit in the Post Office, so what were the options? One was to institute a plan that would eliminate the deficit. That could be done by cutting back services and by laying off workers. That was one option.
The other option with which the previous Government had toyed at one time was to expand the services of the Post Office; in other words, to increase the revenues of the Post Office, not by increasing the cost of the service but by increasing the number of services the public could take advantage of through the Post Office.

Good idea.

May 12, 1988
Supply

It is an excellent idea. When I was in Switzerland two summers ago at an ILO conference, I took a couple of hours to go to the post office in Geneva to see how that post office is run. When I walked into the post office, I thought I was in a McDonald's restaurant. There were advertisements for McDonald's burgers and for Burger King burgers. The local department store was also advertising in the post office. I asked the postmaster what was going on. He told me that they raise millions of dollars in revenues from permitting those advertisements.
What is wrong with cancelling mail with a stamped advertisement? If the stamp is for Sears' 50th anniversary sale, that stamp could be put on cancelled letters and would be distributed across Canada. Who would complain about that form of revenue for the Post Office? It is a simple idea.
What about letting people pay their utility bills at the post office? Why is all that baksheesh left for the big banks? I recall a time when at the post office, people could actually deposit money in their savings accounts. However, nobody now is suggesting that the Post Office go into the banking business.
Surely clients of the Post Office ought to be able to pay their utility bills at the post office. That option was not followed, however. The Government did not tell the Post Office to find new sources of revenue.
After months and months of dithering, the Government handed the post office a business plan in which Canada Post was instructed to cut jobs by 15 per cent, 8,700 jobs. It was to close 5,200 rural post offices across Canada. It was to then embark on the favourite saw of the Conservative Government, privatization. In fact, that is the hidden agenda of this Government. It wants to privatize Canada Post. That is its ultimate aim. Every time a Conservative rises to say that that is not so, we know that it is so because every time they say no, it means yes.
Canada Post was also told to embark on a system of supermailboxes in urban communities. The Government has a fixation about the deficit rather than about what ought to have been the more positive approach which is how to increase revenues for the Post Office.
If it were up to me, I would have said something to all the top echelon people at Canada Post, people who are paid piles of money and have Ph.D.s from business schools and set up business models for the post office. None of them have ever worked on the line. They do not know what it is to work on the line. They do not know what the occupational health and safety record of Canada Post is. They never see the conditions in which those people eat lunch. They are the ones who say that the employees have to check their purses because they cannot go on the job with their purses. They do not have to check their wallets or briefcases. They go to their nice, posh offices and sit around. They get their nice big cheques every two weeks.
I would have said to those people: "You go out and come back with a plan showing how we can raise revenues. I don't want to hear about cut-backs in services and I don't want to hear about raising the cost of postage stamps and mail services. I want creative ideas for how the Post Office can earn more revenues, that is what I want to hear. That is music to my ears, not this stuff that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs loves to hear, privatize, privatize, cut back, cut back".
Let me deal with a couple more things. I have heard it said that it is only members of the NDP who are complaining about the supermailboxes. The Minister who spoke earlier said that we suggested rural folk ought to have door-to-door delivery. Small town Canada ought to have door-to-door delivery. This Party has not said that. None of our speakers in this debate said that. What we are talking about are those urban communities where one side of the street is getting door-to-door delivery and the other side has to use supermailboxes. These boxes are monstrosities. Not only are they an inconvenience, they have created a class system within urban communities. On one side we have door-to-door delivery, on the other we have supermailboxes.
Is it just the NDP who are complaining and saying we do not want supermailboxes? No one in their right mind would suggest that the Peterborough City Council is made up of raving democratic socialists. I hardly think so. Yet that council sent a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) saying that it does not endorse the installation of supermailboxes in urban subdivisions. Canada Post has given the council until May 13 to comply with the request. "If it refuses, Canada Post Corporation will have no alternative but to redeploy resources for implementation in other communities". That is Mr. William Lockman, to the manager of the supermailboxes. He is Mr. Superbox. He wrote that in a letter to the mayor of Peterborough.
One of the aldermen on the Peterborough City Council said: "I am shocked by Canada Post's attitude. I didn't realize to what length they'd go to ensure our participation in the supermailbox program." He is speaking for the community of Peterborough.
Again, is it just the NDP that is saying the Government is wrong in discontinuing door-to-door delivery in urban communities and putting in supermailboxes instead? I hardly think so. The Coalition of Handicapped Persons in Canada had this to say: "The supermailbox is one more case of people with disabilities taking a step backward. Once again they have to turn to others for help. Canada Post thinks that simply providing lower mailboxes makes mail more accessible to disabled people. They are defining what is accessible but we know what is accessible." That is an organization particularly concerned with the establishment of the supermailboxes.
May 12, 1988

Another interesting article comes from Mississauga, again an area not known for its raving democratic socialists. This article appeared in The Globe and Mail on March 22 and it says "Postman Never Rings in New Subdivisions". It goes on to point out that when this gentleman has to pick up his mail he has to get in his car, fight traffic for five miles and hope he will find a parking space near the busy intersection where the post office is located. He says that he pays the same taxes and the same price for a postage stamp as everyone else. Why can he not get the same service as everyone else? In British Columbia, a group organized to fight the establishment of supermailboxes says it is a step backward, not a step forward.
In my long period of time here, first as postal critic and then just observing the Post Office scene for years, I came to the conclusion that the major problem with Canada Post has to be its industrial relations, the relationship between the workers and management. Imagine if you can that there are in the order of 36,000 grievances in the Post Office. When the workers win a grievance at first or second stage, Canada Post appeals it all the way through the process. They have a backlog of 36,000 grievances. Do you understand the cost to the taxpayers of resolving those grievances? A lot of them could have been avoided in the first place if there was a more understanding, a more sensitive management in the Post Office.
Just to give one example of the stupidity of the Post Office, they have a new rule now that workers on the line cannot take their purses on the job.
Why?

According to Canada Post, there is theft and this is its way of avoiding that. There is also alcoholism and drug use on the job and this is the way Canada Post will keep it off the line. Yet in the very next breath a spokesman for Canada Post said they have less than 1/2 per cent theft in the Post Office. If someone wants to smuggle drugs on to the line you do not need a purse to put them in. What do they do next? Do they have a man pull his pockets out and leave them out on the line? Do we have them sort mail naked? Do we send in some of those goons to do a body search?
Post Office management in its relationship with its workers has to be somewhere in the Middle Ages. I have seen it time and time again. The bulk of Post Office problems stem from that kind of Neanderthal thinking on the part of management. There are no modern techniques being used. Maybe we should send them all down to that new Honda plant in Alliston. Maybe they might learn a few things about how to treat people.
