CONTROL CENTRE-GOVERNMENT POSITION/ REQUEST FOR MINISTER TO INTERVENE

Mr. Speaker, my comments this evening are further to a question I directed to the Minister of Transport, concerning information I was given by CN employees in Montreal to the effect that the switching yard control centre might be transferred from Montreal to Toronto. Imagine the impact this would have on employees, especially those with families and children of school age who would have to move the whole family, sell their house and go to Toronto, and there is also the language aspect. To realize what the impact would be in this respect, I think we should remember the case of les Gens de I'air, our air traffic controllers. Employees at CN have more or less the same responsibilities, except that they are responsible for railway traffic.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister's reply, if we can call it that, was that he was not aware of anything or at least gave the impression he did not know what was going on. The Minister's behaviour and his attitude were certainly not new. As far as Quebec is concerned, we got much the same reaction when discussing the safety aspects of the Jacques-Cartier Bridge and the Champlain Bridge. Today, the Minister of Transport happens to be from Quebec, but I must say that the response has not been any more satisfactory to Quebecers who are seeking assurances or formal guarantees that these jobs will remain in Montreal and will not be transferred to Toronto. There is another issue which concerns a contract for building locomotives, and this particular contract for thirty locomotives was awarded to a company in the United States, while it is common knowledge that CN headquarters are in Montreal and that Bombardier's locomotive workshops are in Montreal East.
CN, which is a Crown corporation, just happened to award contracts to the United States instead of letting Quebecers do the job, and the Minister didn't have the gumption to answer my question. If he is so reluctant to have the contract revised to give Bombardier the order for thirty locomotives, I think that, since General Electric in the United States has previously worked with Bombardier, the Canadian content of the thirty locomotives that will be built in the United States should be at least as high as 60 per cent and that Bombardier, which has expertise in engine manufacturing, should make the engines, and the assembly work could be done in Montreal East.
Unfortunately, I have yet to receive a satisfactory reply and the same applies to the possible transfer of jobs now located in

May 12, 1988
Adjournment Debate
Montreal. The reason given was the need for modernizing equipment. To do this, and in connection with the federal Government's deregulation legislation, what I call the law of the jungle, the CN now says that what counts is cutting costs, and bilingualism certainly costs money. Since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister want to cut costs, all operations will be concentrated in Toronto. Only one language will be used. They can put in a bilingual employee who can talk to the people in rural Quebec, but it makes no sense to appoint someone to work in French in Canada. That is just for Quebec, and even in Quebec some can be bilingual and that should be enough.
Mr. Speaker, let me tell you, and the Parliamentary Secretary who is about to reply, that Quebecers will not stand for this. We can take care of ourselves. Recently we had Queen Beatrix who came to tell us about the Durham Report-we can see the federal Government's attitude, but we will never let ourselves be assimilated! We will never lose those jobs! We refused to separate. But if it doesn't work out, Mr. Speaker, we could tell the rest of the country that if they don't take us as we are, we will go elsewhere.
I hope that we will not come to such conclusions and that the Conservative Government will realize the linguistic importance of Quebec and guarantee French-language jobs in Quebec will stay there. We don't object to the upgrading of equipment in Toronto, Montreal or Winnipeg. Even Montreal workers agree. In order to maintain linguistic duality in Canada and preserve the French language in Quebec, the Federal Government could order CN to maintain the jobs of switching yard control workers in Montreal and provide any additional funding required to protect those jobs and the French language within CN as well as Canada.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to respond to the Hon. Member with regard to his question of some time ago. Let me begin by referring to a report concerning a 1986 collision between a Via Rail passenger train and a CN freight train at Bernieres, Quebec, which I understand happens to be in the riding of the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine), an outstanding Member of the House of Commons.
The Canadian Transport Commission ordered CN to upgrade the technology of the dispatching control equipment for its St. Lawrence region. The upgraded, computer assisted equipment must be operative by mid-1990. The CTC order calls for a significant financial investment by the railway. A study is currently under way to determine how best to comply with the order.
I would like to remind the Hon. Member that, being a Crown corporation, CN has an obligation to the federal Government and to Canadian taxpayers to operate in a safe,
efficient, and profitable manner. A consolidation of the Montreal centre with the one in Toronto is being examined, but it is only one of the many options being considered. The railway has not completed its examination and no decision has been taken.
The perception that Montreal, as the Canadian hub of transportation, may lose its pre-eminent role is indeed not correct. CN's employment level in Montreal and in the Province of Quebec, expressed as a percentage of total workforce, has remained virtually unchanged at about 25 per cent to 26 per cent. With regard to the use of French as the language of communication for train operations in Quebec, the Government has already expressed its concern to CN in this matter. I am confident that such concerns will be very carefully considered by CN before it makes its final decision.
Finally, I would like to remind the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie	(Mr. Malepart) that Crown
corporations have the legal and financial scope, authority, and responsibility to manage their own affairs without interference from the Government.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 29, 1988,1 asked the Minister of Finance of Canada (Mr. Wilson) to comment on a report of the Conference Board concerning our economic situation in general. Since oral question period does not lend itself to developing a particular theme, I want to take these few minutes to explain further the Conference Board's position, which is also shared by the editorialists of various specialized magazines in the country on our economy, by the major banks, in other words by those who make economic decisions and ensure that Canadians have a good standard of living.
For example, it is mentioned there that interest rates have gone down by 4 per cent since 1984.
This means that someone with a $50,000 mortgage saves $2,000 a year or $166 a month because we have created a climate favorable to lower interest rates.
Mr. Speaker, take another example. If you have a car that cost you $12,000 and your interest rate is 4 per cent lower, that means you save $40 every month. Since it normally takes 36 months to pay for a car, the savings are substantial.
Low interest rates are beneficial not only for consumers but also for producers, business people, and entrepreneurs. It is important to have lower interest expenses when you want to expand or launch a new business. This too is possible, thanks to our good, sound management.
We also said in this report that we helped control inflation. Those who have thought back to 1970, 1975 and 1980 recall that in those years, the purchasing power of Canadians

May 12, 1988

declined 10, 12, 13 per cent a year. Increasingly, the same $100 bought less groceries or rented a smaller house or apartment and this especially affected older people, Mr. Speaker. We had a smaller car, shorter outings, less travel, because the Canadian dollar, due to the interventionist, spendthrift policies of the socialists and Liberals... In other words, Canadians were spending money they did not have. This weakened the Canadian dollar and reduced the savings of the elderly.
The report also indicates that we have very well managed our deficit. It is for this reason and also because the Canadian Government has borrowed less that interest rates are down. Fewer are the Canadians who want to borrow, cheaper is the money. We have succeeded in creating a climate where money is cheaper. We have done that by making very good use of the taxpayers' money.
Finally, the report mentions two other points: First our tax reform. Since 1917, nobody had ever heard of income tax coming down following a tax reform. So it is the first time since 1917 that 85 per cent of Canadian taxpayers will pay less income tax because of a tax reform; it is the first time that 90 per cent of senior citizens in Canada will no longer pay income tax. What does this mean? It means more money available for Canadian taxpayers and, what is more important, more money for contractors and businessmen who, realizing that the State has become a less demanding partner with a possibility to pay less income tax on their benefits, will expand their businesses further.
Finally, the Conference Board of Canada emphasized that the Government had signed with the United States a trade deal which would make it possible for our manufacturers to be protected through secured access to the American market. As you know, one Canadian out of five is working because of the goods we are exporting to foreign markets. One Canadian out of four is working because of the goods we are exporting to the United States. Our exports to the United States amount to $95 billion a year. That means jobs!
And this market is being jeopardized because the Americans are having problems with their balance of payments and they have decided to stop some of our exports, including lumber, hogs, salted fish, and all sorts of goods when they cross the U.S. border. We have decided to streamline Canada-United States relations and prevent any unilateral action on the part of our American neighbours through a Free Trade Agreement. It is this agreement which will increase our market in the United States by as many as 250 million customers.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I see that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Vincent) is here to reply. If possible, I should like him to tell Canadians what would have happened if, instead of having a Conservative Government which is aware of the value of money, of the need for an economic recovery, we had lived again under a Liberal-Socialist coalition, meaning indiscriminate spending, money squandering, uncontroled borrowing, no new businesses, no
Adjournment Debate
new jobs, no trade with the United States and increased employment. What would have happened, Mr. Speaker? This is the question I am directing to the Parliament Secretary to the Minister of Finance, my friend the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend my colleague the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) for the outstanding job he has been doing since 1984 here in the House of Commons and in his riding. We know that he is a well known and experienced administrator who, before jumping into the political arena, had a brilliant career. I am sure he will also have a brilliant career on the political scene.
As I listened to my colleague from Levis talk about economic matters, I could appreciate that indeed he has worked in that sector before, and since 1984 he has been keeping a close watch on everything the Government has done.
Mr. Speaker, he is right when he says that the Conference Board projections have been revised upwards. Like most other trend indicators who predicted a better economic performance throughout the country, they proved to be wrong: Canada's performance has been even better than expected.
When my colleague from Levis talks about the Opposition and a coalition, whether it is a coalition or either one of the other two Parties in office, we see and we know their forecasts. Mr. Speaker, like my colleague from Levis, I am sure you too recall that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tabled the documents of his 1984 economic statement, both the Leader of the Official Opposition and the Leader of the New Democratic Party said that we would lose hundreds of thousands of jobs. Mr. Speaker, jobs were created in 1984.
When he tabled his Budget in May 1985, the reaction was the same: Both Opposition leaders said the Budget would make us lose jobs. Mr. Speaker, jobs were created in 1985.
When the Budgets came out in 1986, 1987 and 1988, all we could hear from the two Opposition leaders-Liberal or NDP, it does not matter-was that we would lose jobs, it was bad for Canada, and what have you. Those were negative remarks which failed to take the Canadian reality into consideration, Mr. Speaker. My colleague from Levis knows what the Canadian reality is. He is living it, he works with the Government, he makes constructive comments, he takes a positive approach. That is what has been done by the Conservative Government since 1984.
Mr. Speaker, nearly 1,300,000 jobs have been created since 1984, although every time this Government tabled bills with an impact on the economy, the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) and the Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner) made dire predictions that jobs would be lost. Every time we presented major projects, such as the free trade agreement...

May 12, 1988
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, everyone agrees the agreement will create jobs in this country and protect existing jobs.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) says he will tear up the agreement. Mr. Speaker, even a child of six can see the Leader of the Opposition doesn't have the strength to tear up the agreement. He can't even lead his own caucus, much less tear up the agreement. The Leader of the NDP, who has enjoyed the benefits of free trade in his riding for twenty years, also says the agreement is no good for Canada. So what is good for Oshawa isn't good for Canada? Come on, Mr. Speaker!
I appreciate the positive comments made by the Hon. Member for Levis and, in concluding, Mr. Speaker, I again wish to congratulate the Hon. Member on the excellent work he has done in the House of Commons and in his riding.

ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-NITROGEN OXIDE EMISSIONS- DISCUSSIONS IN GENEVA/POSITION OF UNITED STATES

Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to pursue a question about emissions that cause acid rain, particularly nitrogen oxide emissions. This is an extremely important question. We are beginning to make some progress in Canada on the sulphur emissions that cause acid rain, but a very important question for acid rain is the so-called NO, emissions.
Negotiations have been ongoing in Geneva about this matter-and a draft protocol has been circulated-for quite a while. We are trying to find out where they are and to what extent the Americans, who are a major source of NOx emissions in Canada and a major source of acid rain and other health problems, are responsible.
We find that the Government's response is that all is well and that we are making progress. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), when asked a question by the Leader of the New Democratic Party, said that we had a win in Geneva in the negotiations. What were the Americans trying to do in Geneva? They were trying to get something into the protocol stating that instead of choosing 1987 as the year against which a freeze in emissions would have to be measured, they could choose any year. They could take an earlier year. They took the year 1978. Their emissions were higher then, so they would be able to increase their emissions by 10 per cent and still not violate the protocol.
Increases in these emissions would be extremely dangerous for Canada. The increase they would be allowed would be the same amount as the total emissions for Canada itself. What good would it do for us to decrease our emissions if the Americans could increase theirs? It is very important to get this loophole out of the protocol. However, there was no win.
When I asked the question of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) subsequently, he said that the Americans could have chosen 1978, their highest year, and that we
had eliminated the clause "any previous year". He referred to another proposal and said: "It is a double win for Canada".
Earlier today I had the opportunity to raise this question at the committee studying acid rain with the officials of the Department. They conceded that this question of taking out the previous year had not been agreed upon by the Americans. Further discussions are going on. The Americans are taking the matter back to their Government from Geneva. We will not know until Canada Day, July I, whether the Americans will agree. We also found out that the Americans are objecting to some very basic approaches to this question. They are not so sure they want to look at critical loadings. They are not quite sure about the accuracy of using those.
I have questions about critical loadings as well. They may be too generous in allowing emissions. We do not have very thorough information about the health consequences as opposed to the consequences for lakes and forests. We know less about the human health consequences. It is possible that we should be allowing even fewer emissions than we are.
It is also true that the American are resisting the measurement of transboundary fluxes. They are not so sure they agree with our proportions on what amount of their emissions come to Canada and create problems for human health, for lakes and forests, and so forth. We are very far from getting an agreement with the United States when the Americans are not sure about how to measure and how to deal with this question.
We have to realize that NO, emissions are still increasing even with this freeze. With more vehicles on the road, even if we have improved standards, those emissions will go up. We are not even at the stage of reducing emissions. We are hoping to get to a freeze that will come into effect by 1994. These are modest objectives indeed, and we are not sure whether we will get international agreement.
There are four ways NO, causes problems with people. Acid rain is probably the best known. There are also problems of ozone in cities. In the case of Vancouver they are locally produced. In the case of a number of our cities, Windsor along to Toronto up to Montreal, in that corridor, ozone comes from the United States. There are health consequences, respiratory problems, and children are especially vulnerable. We do not have very good data nor estimates on where the danger levels are. We are probably exceeding them very often.
Another problem coming from NO, emissions is nitrous oxide, an ozone depleting substance in the atmosphere having an effect something like that of chlorofluorocarbons on which we have just negotiated the treaty for a reduction over the long term. Nitrous oxide lasts 150 years. It is a very stable substance. It contributes to the greenhouse effect, something we are only beginning to study. We are only beginning to worry about the possibilities of major climate changes, of raising of the oceans' levels, as the swamping of cities on the coast, of making some areas uninhabitable and others drought areas. It would change enormously the climate. We are only beginning
May 12, 1988

to understand the consequences of this aspect of NO, emissions.
We cannot have any optimism that the measures we are even contemplating right now will be adequate.

Mr. Speaker, the Special Committee on Acid Rain will visit Washington in June, which is in a few weeks time, and will be there from June 6 to June 8 to present Canada's policy to the Americans, to Senators, Congressmen and officials. The purpose is to explain to the Americans our specific claims and our concerns about the disastrous effects of acid rain. This visit is particularly important because the Canadian Government is not doing enough to convey our concerns to the Americans. In my view, this is because of the free trade negotiations. The Canadian Government cannot negotiate two agreements at the same time, and I think it is no accident that we do have a free trade agreement and we do not have the agreement we need to regulate and reduce the emissions that cause acid rain.
Mr. Speaker, one of the overriding concerns of Canadians is to reduce emissions that cause acid rain, and the Government must take this concern seriously.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the negotiations in the Economic Commission for Europe, the ECE, to draft a protocol to control nitrogen oxide emissions are nearing completion. The officials testified at our acid rain committee meeting today, that special committee of the House of Commons, and those officials representing the Canadian Government are to be commended for their negotiations in Geneva. On July 1, 1988, Canada will declare its intentions concerning its signature of this protocol.
The negotiations in the 35-member ECE have shown Canadians just how justified our claims have been all along when we have called on the Americans to take action on acid rain. Before and during the April 27 and 28 meeting in Geneva, our Government was using every lever available to us to gain the support of the European nations. We asked for their support to ensure that Canada would not fall victim to
Adjournment Debate
increased NO, pollution from the United States as a result of credit language in the draft protocol.
It appeared as if the Europeans might be willing to accept a protocol that would result in increased damage to Canada's environment, just to bring the Americans into the protocol. Thankfully, this did not happen. The Europeans supported us because they too recognized the dangerous precedent this would have set for all future international environmental law. The Americans were sent a very clear message that they should join the international fight against acid rain.
The draft protocol now contains no credit clause. Canada's proposal to delete the so-called American credit clause was supported by all but the U.S. delegation. The phrase "any previous year" is now in square brackets, meaning that it is still being considered, and is qualified by another square-bracketed phrase which states that there will be no increase in transboundary fluxes from the 1987 level for the period between 1987 and 1996. Again, Canada's position was supported.
If the U.S. signs the protocol, Canada will have earned a complete freeze on transboundary fluxes until the second step of the protocol is in place in 1996. In this situation we will have succeeded in eliminating any negative effects on Canada of the use of any previous year as the baseline for freezing emissions. The second step in the protocol requires the establishment of critical loads, reductions required to meet those critical loads, and measures and a time-table commencing no later than January 1, 1996 to achieve the reduction. The review process required by the protocol will ensure that the second step goals are in fact met.
Our experience in Geneva has shown yet again that Canada is not only a valued member but a leader of the world community in the fight against air pollution. We put our case forcefully to the Europeans and we won. We will continue to press our case with the Americans on acid rain. The world community is on our side.
